default.p.15day_n3-t30-p1.vietnamese:
Robot Vacuum Cleaners

Robot vacuum cleaners are said to have been selling very well recently.

When we are busy, we often have no time to vacuum and clean the house properly, do we?

At times like that, it is extremely convenient if a robot vacuum cleaner can clean for us.

Once its schedule is set, a robot vacuum cleaner will clean even when we are away from home, and because it operates quietly, it can finish cleaning while we are asleep.

Moreover, it is said that after cleaning, the robot vacuum cleaner automatically recharges its battery.

With one of these, it seems that we could live in a clean house all year round.

default.p.15day_n3-t31-p1.vietnamese:
Preventive measures
In Japan, from February to April, people wearing face masks are often seen.
During this season, pollen floats in the air, and when it enters the mouth or nose, it can cause a sore throat, a runny nose, or sneezing.
This condition is called “pollen allergy” (Kafunshō).
To prevent pollen allergy, many people wear face masks when going outside.
The following advice is often given about drying laundry as one preventive measure against pollen allergy.
First, laundry should be dried indoors.
If it is dried outdoors, it is reportedly better to hang it out as early as possible in the morning and bring it inside during the morning, because this makes it less likely that pollen will stick to the clothes.
The reason is said to be that pollen is more likely to scatter between noon and 3:00 p.m., when the temperature rises.

default.p.15day_n3-t32-p1.vietnamese:
Flower Viewing

When people think of spring in Japan, most Japanese people probably imagine cherry blossoms.
When the cherry blossoms bloom, people take part in “flower viewing,” such as eating boxed lunches or drinking alcohol under cherry trees in parks.
Recently, “flower viewing” seems to have become popular not only among Japanese people but also among foreign visitors.
It is said that in recent years, the number of foreign tourists visiting Japan has been increasing from late March, when the cherry blossoms begin to bloom, through early April.
It would be wonderful if more and more people came to understand Japanese culture through “flower viewing.”

default.p.15day_n3-t33-p1.vietnamese:
Vegetables
「Why are salads at fast-food restaurants and set-meal restaurants so small and yet so expensive? If that's the case, I might as well order something else, like french fries or a meat dish」...
When I was younger, I used to think that way.
Surprisingly, now that I have turned 30, I actively order salad.
At this age, I care more about my health than I did in the past.

default.p.15day_n3-t35-p1.vietnamese:
When memorizing new vocabulary
How do you usually study new vocabulary or kanji?
Here are some tips to help even people who are not good at memorizing remember things easily.
First, when memorizing something, we should try to provide the brain with as many stimuli as possible.
For example, when learning a new word, instead of merely looking at the textbook, you will remember it much more firmly if you read it aloud while writing it on paper.
This is because the mouth, ears, and hands are stimulated simultaneously along with the eyes.
Studying new words while tossing a ball back and forth also stimulates various parts of the body, making it very effective.
After learning something new, get a good night’s sleep. People often think that sleeping may cause them to forget, but the opposite is true.
The human brain is structured to firmly retain what it has learned during sleep.

default.p.15day_n3-t36-p1.vietnamese:
How People Work and Rest
Japanese people are often said to work too much.
So, does Japan have fewer public holidays than other countries around the world?
In fact, when we look into it, Japan has 16 public holidays a year, which is reportedly the sixth-highest number in the world.
Since the country with the most public holidays has 18, it seems that Japan does not necessarily have too few holidays.
Then why do Japanese people end up working so much?
The reason seems to lie in the difference in the number of paid vacation days.
In places such as Europe, where there are relatively few public holidays, taking a long vacation, or “vacance,” is established by law, allowing workers to take extended time off to refresh themselves.
In compensation for that, they can devote themselves fully to their work.
In Japan, on the other hand, not only are there relatively few paid vacation days, but many people also feel unable to take time off comfortably.
Many people say things like, “I cannot be the only one taking time off when everyone around me is working,” or “If I take time off, the work will pile up, so I cannot do it.”
I think it would be good if, as in countries with long vacations, it became normal for everyone to take time off together during a certain period.

default.p.15day_n3-t37-p1.vietnamese:
Masks
One thing that surprises foreigners visiting Japan is the large number of people who wear masks.
Usually, when people see someone wearing a mask, they probably assume that the person has a cold or flu, is trying to prevent one, or has a pollen allergy.
However, a recent trend among young people is wearing masks to hide personal imperfections.
Specifically, they wear them when they have not put on makeup or are worried about bad breath.
In addition, more people are wearing masks to avoid communicating with others, saying things such as, “Wearing a mask makes me less noticeable” and “Other people cannot tell what I am thinking.”
It is said that anxiety when one does not have a mask may indicate a lack of self-confidence or a strong inferiority complex.
Wearing a mask is not necessarily bad, but if being without one causes problems in daily life, one should consider consulting a doctor.

default.p.15day_n3-t38-p1.vietnamese:
A Town I Want to Live In
The other day, my job transfer was finalized.
Taking this opportunity, I also decided to move to make commuting easier.
While looking at websites, I chose a room that met my criteria, such as its exposure to sunlight and size.
Then I asked to be shown some rooms in person, but none of them made me feel, "This is the place I would choose."
The rooms clearly met my requirements, yet I could not picture myself living in any of them.
When I told my friends about it, they said, "Instead of looking for a house you want to live in, why don't you try looking for a town you want to live in?"
No matter how good the house is, if you cannot grow to like the town where you live, you will not be able to enjoy yourself.
This time, in addition to criteria for the room, I looked for a town with many stylish cafés and a convenient library.
As a result, I found a room that I liked very much.
I am extremely excited about my new life in this room.

default.p.15day_n3-t39-p1.vietnamese:
Growing Plants
Recently, I started growing vegetables myself.
I had never been interested in gardening, but a friend invited me, saying, “Why don't we rent a plot of land from the city and grow something together?”
Tilling the soil to soften it, watering the plants every day, and pulling weeds around them were all hard tasks, so at first I thought I should never have started.
However, as I cared for the plants day after day, I became happy to see the vegetables grow, and before I knew it, going to the plot had become enjoyable.
Although it was only a small thing, I was truly moved when I harvested the vegetables for the first time.
Moreover, I was amazed by how delicious the vegetables I had grown myself were.
I have heard that growing plants is good for both physical and mental health.
Because we exercise our bodies every day, we do not lack physical activity, and looking forward eagerly to the harvest allows us to nurture hope for the future.

Dear Ms. Misaki Nakata,
It has been a long time. How have you been?
Last week, while on a business trip to Tokyo, I had some free time, so I visited our university for the first time since graduating.
The area in front of the station has been redeveloped, and compared with five years ago, the atmosphere has become quite lively.
During my time studying abroad, you helped me so much, Ms. Misaki.
When I was having trouble writing my graduation thesis, I do not think I could have graduated without your help.
To me, you are my second teacher.
Even now, I am truly very grateful to you.
If I have another opportunity to visit Japan, next time I would like to go all the way to Hokkaido to see you.
Until then, I hope you stay healthy.
Wang Jinxiang

default.p.15day_n3-t41-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, signs such as “Please stand in two lines on the escalator” have begun to appear at train stations.

Although station escalators are wide enough for two people to stand side by side, in most cases people stand only on the left (note).

The right side is left open so that people in a hurry can pass through.

Recently, however, railway companies have begun encouraging people to stand in two lines because “standing in two lines is safer.”

It is true that doing so is safer.

Thinking this, I actually tried standing on the right the other day, but immediately became an obstacle to the people coming up behind me.

Habits that have continued for many years are not easy to change, even when we intend to change them.

If standing in two lines becomes common, perhaps that will still be a very distant prospect.

(Note) Depending on the region, the left and right sides may be reversed.

Have you ever heard the saying “A messy room reflects a troubled state of mind”?
People say that a cluttered, untidy room reflects the mind of the person living there.
It is also thought that when our minds are filled with negative emotions, we lose interest in cleaning, and as a result, the room becomes messy.
Then, when we look at the messy room, we feel irritated or accumulate even more stress.
We cannot immediately find the things we want to use.
This makes us even more frustrated... and the cycle repeats itself in a vicious circle.
Whenever I think, “I may be a little stressed lately” or “My room has become messier than before,” I decide to start by cleaning my room.

Chocolate
The other day, I bought a box of chocolate at a convenience store whose packaging looked rather unusual.
From the packaging, it was impossible to tell that it was chocolate at all. It was a little expensive, but the package was very attractive and stylish.
While I was eating it during lunch break at school, my friend told me, “That has been extremely popular lately.”
According to her, this chocolate had been sold once several years ago, but apparently it had not sold very well.
However, after spending several years redesigning the chocolate and its packaging for women and putting it back on the market, the chocolate reportedly sold astonishingly well.

default.p.15day_n3-t44-p1.vietnamese:
Rice Balls (Onigiri)
Recently, I asked an international student, 「What surprised you most when you came to Japan?」.
The answer was 「rice balls」.
I had asked other students the same question before, but since I had received answers such as 「The streets are clean,」 「Vending machines are convenient,」 and 「Trains run on time,」 I instinctively asked in response, 「Why rice balls?」.
According to the student:
The reasons are as follows:
First, they are easy to buy at convenience stores, and because they are compact, they can be kept in a bag.
Second, they can be eaten immediately whenever you want, and they are more filling than bread.
Third, there are many different flavors. Apparently, after trying one once, the student bought them many more times.
Rice balls really are an excellent fast food.
I also like them very much.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) そんな
The demonstrative 「そんな」combines with 「とき」to form 「そんなとき」(“at times like that”), referring back to the previously mentioned state of being too busy to clean.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q1.explanation: In the passage, the author begins by stating a common reality: 「忙しいときは、なかなか掃除機をかける時間がありませんよね。」 (When you are busy, you hardly have time to vacuum, do you?). Grammatically, the prenominal modifier 「そんな」 combines directly with a noun (here, 「そんなとき」) and means “such” or “like that.” It functions as a context-dependent demonstrative (文脈指示), summarizing the entire nature of the busy situation just mentioned. When inserted into the sentence 「そんなとき、お掃除ロボットが自分にかわって掃除をしてくれたら、とっても便利です。」, the complete meaning is: “At times like that, it would be extremely convenient if a robot vacuum could clean in my place.” To distinguish the choices, remember that information just mentioned in the passage requires the 「そ」 series, immediately ruling out 「あの」 and 「あんな」. Also distinguish 「そのとき」, which refers to a specific time or moment (“then,” “at that time”), from 「そんなとき」, the natural expression for a similar type of situation or circumstance (“at times like that”).
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) 「その」 usually refers to a specific, definite point in time (“at that time”), so it is unsuitable for referring to a general type of situation or state (“in situations like that”) in this context.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q1.why.1: ✓ (b) 「そんな」 directly modifies the noun 「とき」 to form 「そんなとき」(at times like that), linking the sentences and accurately referring back to the recently mentioned busy situation.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) 「あの」 belongs to the A-series demonstratives and is used only when both the speaker and listener clearly know the matter in question from reality. It is not used to refer to content just mentioned in the context.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) 「あんな」 also belongs to the A-series demonstratives, referring to something both parties already know. Therefore, it cannot connect newly introduced information in the article.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) かわって
The grammar pattern 「N にかわって」 means “instead of N” or “in place of N,” accurately expressing that a robot vacuum does the cleaning instead of the speaker when they are busy.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q2.explanation: Based on the sentence in the passage: 「（そんな）とき、お掃除ロボットが自分に（　2　）掃除をしてくれたら、とっても便利です。」, the preceding context clearly describes a situation in which being busy leaves almost no time to vacuum. Thus, the speaker wishes for something to do the cleaning in their place. The key N3 grammar pattern here is 「N にかわって / にかわり」, which attaches directly to a noun and means “instead of, in place of N.” It is commonly used when a person or thing performs an action in place of the person or thing originally responsible for that role or task. Learners may easily confuse the four choices because they all combine with 「に」, but remember this distinction: 「にしたがって」 expresses following instructions or a corresponding change (“as...”), 「にくわえて」 adds something (“in addition to”), and 「によって」 indicates a method, cause, or classification (“depending on”). Therefore, only 「かわって」 expresses the idea of “doing the housework in someone’s place.” The completed sentence means: “At times like that, it would be really convenient if a robot vacuum could clean in my place.”
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q2.why.0: ✓ (a) The structure 「N にかわって」means “instead of N” or “in place of N,” correctly expressing that the cleaning robot replaces the user when they are busy.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) The structure 「N にしたがって」means “in accordance with N” or “as …, …,” so it does not fit the meaning of this context at all.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) The structure 「N にくわえて」means “in addition to N” or “besides N.” It is incorrect here because the speaker wants the robot to do the cleaning instead of doing it together.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) The structure 「N によって」 indicates means, cause, or “depending on N”; it cannot express the idea of taking over someone’s work.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) あいだに
The pattern 「〜ている間に」 describes a completed action, such as 掃除を終わらせる, taking place while another state, such as 寝ている, is continuing.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q3.explanation: The passage contains the sentence: 「お掃除ロボットは時間をセットすれば、留守中でも掃除をしてくれますし、音が静かなので、寝ている（　3　）掃除を終わらせることもできます。」 (If you set the time, the robot vacuum will clean even while you are away, and because it operates quietly, it can also finish cleaning while you are asleep.) The key grammar pattern is 「V-ている + あいだに」, which indicates that an action takes place and is completed during a period in which another state is continuing. The following clause uses 「掃除を終わらせる」, expressing the completion of an action, so adding 「に」 after「あいだ」is correct. For the exam, remember that「あいだに」goes with a completed or punctual action, unlike「あいだ」or「〜にわたって」, which require an action or state that continues throughout the entire period. It also differs from「〜にかけて」, which must form a range from a starting point to an ending point (〜から〜にかけて).
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) The pattern 「〜にかけて」 indicates an approximate range from one point to another and usually accompanies 「〜から」. It does not combine with a single state marker such as 「寝ている」.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「〜にわたって」describes something continuing throughout an entire period and does not go with a conclusive action such as 「終わらせる」.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q3.why.2: ✓ (c) The pattern 「V-ている + あいだに」 describes an action involving a specific point in time or completion (掃除を終わらせる) that occurs while another state continues.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q3.why.3: ✗ (d) The pattern 「〜うえに」 means “in addition” or “not only... but also...” and adds supplementary information; it does not indicate when an action takes place.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) しかも
The conjunction 「しかも」 means “moreover” or “on top of that.” It adds another positive feature to the series of advantages mentioned in the previous sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q4.explanation: Based on the passage, the preceding sentence lists several conveniences of a robot vacuum: 「お掃除ロボットは時間をセットすれば、留守中でも掃除をしてくれますし、音が静かなので、寝ているあいだに掃除を終わらせることもできます。」. Therefore, the complete sentence with 「しかも」 is 「しかも掃除が終わったら、お掃除ロボットが自分で充電を行うそうです。」, meaning: “Moreover, apparently the robot vacuum charges itself once it has finished cleaning.” Grammatically, the conjunction 「しかも」 begins a sentence that adds another fact or feature in the same direction—usually another positive or another negative point—with the sense of “on top of that.” An important test-taking distinction is between 「しかも」 and 「しかし」, whose kana forms look similar: if the following information adds another positive point, choose 「しかも」, not a contrasting conjunction such as 「しかし」 or 「けれども」.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q4.why.0: ✗ (a) 「しかし」 is a conjunction expressing opposition or contrast (“however”), whereas the following sentence does not contrast with the advantages mentioned.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q4.why.1: ✓ (b) 「しかも」 adds further information in the same direction, meaning “moreover” or “what is more.” It is exactly right for introducing the additional advantage of automatic battery charging.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) 「それとも」means “or” and is used to connect alternatives in an interrogative sentence; it is not used to add information in a declarative sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) 「けれども」expresses concession or contrast (“but”), so it does not fit a passage that continues praising the convenience of robots.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q5.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) さえあれば
The pattern 「～さえ～ば」expresses the only necessary condition, meaning “as long as there is...” or “if one only has...”. It fits the idea that having this vacuum cleaner alone is enough to keep the house clean all year.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q5.explanation: The evidence is in the final sentence of the passage: 「これ（　5　）、一年中きれいな家で過ごせそうですね。」The blank requires a structure used with the demonstrative pronoun 「これ」to form the key N3 pattern 「Noun + さえあれば」, combining the emphatic particle さえ with the conditional form of あります. This pattern means "as long as there is..." or "all you need is..." It emphasizes a minimum or essential condition that will make the desired result possible. The complete sentence 「これさえあれば、一年中きれいな家で過ごせそうですね。」translates as: "As long as we have this (robot vacuum), it looks like we can enjoy living in a clean house all year round, don’t you think?" To avoid confusing it with choice (a), 「があればあるほど」(the more there is...), focus on the logic: one vacuum cleaner is enough to handle the cleaning, so this is not a quantity-based progression like 「～ば～ほど」.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q5.why.0: ✗ (a) The pattern 「～ば～ほど」 means “the more..., the more...,” which does not fit the semantic logic of this context.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q5.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「～といえば」means “speaking of” or “when one mentions,” and is used to introduce a topic or association. It is not used to state a hypothetical condition.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q5.why.2: ✗ (c) 「～によれば」 means “according to...” and is used to introduce a source of information. It does not fit with the conjectural expression 「～そうですね」 in the following clause.
default.q.15day_n3-t30-q5.why.3: ✓ (d) The pattern「～さえあれば」means “as long as there is...,” accurately expressing the minimum condition needed to live in a clean house all year round.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 見かけます
The transitive verb「見かける」combines with the particle「を」to express casually seeing or coming across someone in everyday life.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q1.explanation: The opening sentence is 「日本では２月～４月に、マスクをしている人をよく（　1　）。」, indicating that the passage describes people commonly seen wearing masks during the pollen season. The completed sentence means: "In Japan, from February to April, you often see people wearing masks." 「見かける」, whose polite form is 「見かけます」, is a transitive verb used with を in 「[person/thing] を見かける」. It means to happen to see someone or something, without having intentionally looked for it. 「見える」is an intransitive verb used with が for something that comes into view naturally. 「見られる」describes having the opportunity to watch or view something, such as a film or flowers. Therefore, when the object is a person marked by を, only 「見かける」forms a natural sentence. 「見かけられます」, whether passive or potential, does not fit the active structure with を here.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) 「見えます」is an intransitive verb describing an image naturally coming into view, so it requires the particle 「が」, not 「を」.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) 「見られます」means that something can be seen or watched when the necessary conditions are available. It is not used to describe accidentally spotting someone on the street.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) 「見かけます」is a transitive verb meaning to happen to see or come across a person or thing, making it grammatically and semantically correct with the object 「人を」.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) 「見かけられます」is the passive or potential form of 「見かける」and does not fit a sentence in the active voice with the object particle 「を」.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) ために
The structure 「V-る + ために」expresses purpose (“in order to”), fitting the context of wearing a mask to prevent pollen allergies.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q2.explanation: Based on the sentence in the passage: 「花粉症になるのを防ぐ（　2　）、外に出るときはマスクをする人が多いのです。」, the author is explaining why many people wear masks when they go outside. The key grammar pattern is the purpose expression 「V-る / N の + ために」, used with the dictionary-form volitional verb 「防ぐ」to indicate the goal toward which the deliberate action in the following clause is directed. Once completed, the sentence means: “To prevent hay fever, many people wear masks whenever they go outside.” Distinguish it from the tempting option 「ことで」: 「V-る + ために」is used when the following clause describes an action performed to achieve the purpose in the preceding clause, whereas 「ことで」expresses a means or method by which a specific result is achieved.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q2.why.0: ✓ (a) The structure 「V-る + ために」 expresses purpose (“in order to…”), accurately describing wearing a mask to prevent hay fever.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) 「～上に」means “moreover” or “in addition” and adds information in the same direction; it is not used to express purpose.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) Incorrect because 「～によって」follows a noun to indicate a cause or means; it does not directly combine with the dictionary-form verb 「防ぐ」to express purpose.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) 「V-る + ことで」means “by doing” or “through doing,” expressing a method or cause leading to a result, not simply a purpose.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) として
The pattern 「～として」 directly combines with the noun phrase 「方法の一つ」 to express the status or role of something as “one of the methods.”
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q3.explanation: The basis for the answer is the sentence: 「花粉症を予防する方法の一つ（　3　）、洗濯物の干し方（　4　）、以下のようなことが言われています。」 Position (3) requires grammar expressing the role of hanging laundry as one representative method of prevention. The key N3 pattern is 「Noun + として」, meaning “in the capacity of” or “as,” used to assign a status, role, or representative example to the preceding noun. In 「方法の一つとして」, it establishes that the following advice about hanging laundry is considered one of the methods for preventing hay fever. Do not confuse it with にとって: 「にとって」 indicates a viewpoint or basis for evaluation, whereas 「として」 identifies a name, status, or role. The complete sentence means: “As one of the methods for preventing hay fever, the following points have been suggested regarding how to hang laundry.”
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) 「ところ」indicates a place or the point in time when an action occurs. It does not directly follow a noun to indicate a status or method.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) 「とは」 is used to define or explain a term or concept, so it does not fit the grammar or meaning of the sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) 「とって」 normally forms 「にとって」 to indicate someone's viewpoint or standpoint; it does not mean a person's status or capacity.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q3.why.3: ✓ (d) 「として」follows the noun 「方法の一つ」and correctly expresses status or role, meaning “as” or “as one of the methods.”
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) について
The grammar pattern 「N について」means “about” or “concerning N,” making it the only correct choice for stating the topic of the predicate 「言われています」at the end of the sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q4.explanation: The original sentence is:「花粉症を予防する方法の一つとして、洗濯物の干し方について、以下のようなことが言われています。」Position (4) comes immediately after the noun「洗濯物の干し方」and before the predicate phrase「～と言われています」. The key N3 grammar pattern is「N + について」(about / concerning N), used in an objective and polite way to specify the topic of speech, thought, or writing. The complete sentence means: "As one way to prevent hay fever, the following things are said about how to hang laundry out to dry." To distinguish it in a test, pay attention to the predicate that follows:「～について言われています」is a fixed expression indicating the topic under discussion, whereas「につれて」must accompany changes in both clauses, and「にしては」expresses an evaluation contrary to what would normally be expected.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q4.why.0: ✓ (a) The grammar 「N について」means “about” or “concerning N,” and it combines naturally with the predicate 「言われています」to introduce the topic under discussion.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「につれて」describes simultaneous change in a corresponding direction (“as...,” “the more...the more...”); it is not used to state a topic.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) This is incorrect because 「にしては」 expresses an evaluation that is contrary to the usual standard or expectation (“for..., surprisingly...”), which does not fit the context.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) The phrase「にして」emphasizes an exceptional degree or links clauses; it does not establish the topic of discussion.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q5.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) うちに
Following a noun combined with 「の」, the grammar pattern 「〜うちに」 describes intentionally taking an action during a period of time before conditions change, here during the morning.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q5.explanation: Based on the sentence in the passage: 「もし外に干す場合は、できるだけ朝早く干して、午前中の（ うちに ）部屋の中に入れたほうが、服に花粉が付きにくいそうです」 and the following sentence explaining that temperatures rise from noon to 3 p.m., making pollen more likely to circulate, the writer clearly recommends bringing the laundry indoors before the afternoon weather begins. The key grammar is 「N + のうちに」 (which can also be used with a dictionary-form verb, negative form, progressive form, or adjective), meaning "while / before it changes, take the opportunity to do something." The complete sentence means: "If you dry clothes outdoors, apparently it is better to hang them out as early as possible in the morning and bring them inside during the morning, so pollen is less likely to stick to them." The key distinction from 「までに」 lies in both nuance and structure: 「〜までに」 indicates a deadline by which an action must be completed (usually directly combined as 「午前中までに」 rather than connected with 「の」), whereas this context of taking advantage of a favorable period can only use 「うちに」.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q5.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜最中に」describes an unexpected event interrupting an action in progress; it is not used for an intentional action or advice to make use of the available time.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q5.why.1: ✓ (b) 「午前中のうちに」accurately expresses the idea of bringing the laundry indoors during the morning, before pollen levels rise after noon.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q5.why.2: ✗ (c) The phrase「〜にかけて」indicates an extended period or area, usually in the pattern「〜から〜にかけて」, so it does not fit the grammar or context.
default.q.15day_n3-t31-q5.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜までに」 indicates a deadline and is used directly with a point in time. It does not combine as 「午前中のまでに」, nor does it convey the sense of taking advantage of a convenient period.
default.q.15day_n3-t32-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) といえば
The structure 「N＋といえば」is the correct grammar pattern for introducing a topic and immediately evoking its most characteristic or representative feature.
default.q.15day_n3-t32-q1.explanation: The original sentence is: 「日本の春（　1　）、日本人の多くが桜の花をイメージすることでしょう。」 Since blank (1) follows the noun 「日本の春」 and the following clause describes a familiar psychological association among Japanese people, the key pattern is 「N ＋ といえば」. Used with a noun or the plain form, it introduces a topic and evokes the most representative or iconic image associated with it: “When Japanese spring is mentioned, most Japanese people will probably think of cherry blossoms.” To avoid confusing it with the distractor 「となると」, remember that 「といえば」 is used for a natural recollection or association, as with イメージする or 思い出す. 「となると」 is used when a hypothetical condition or specific situation causes a change in attitude, concern, or a consequential outcome.
default.q.15day_n3-t32-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) The pattern 「N＋といえば」 means “speaking of N...” and combines perfectly with the following clause, which naturally associates it with Japan’s cherry-blossom symbol of spring.
default.q.15day_n3-t32-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern「〜となると」means “if it comes to...” or “once it comes to...”. It is used when a specific situation leads to hesitation or serious consequences, not to introduce a characteristic association.
default.q.15day_n3-t32-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern 「〜というのは」introduces a definition or concept, usually followed by 〜ことだ, or explains a reason, followed by 〜からだ. It does not fit a context involving an imagined image.
default.q.15day_n3-t32-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The pattern「〜といい」commonly appears in the listing structure「AといいBといい」(both A and B...) or expresses a wish or hope. It is not used by itself after a noun to introduce an associated topic.
default.q.15day_n3-t32-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 行われます
Because the noun 「お花見」 is followed by the particle 「が」, the verb must be in passive form to express that the event is held or takes place.
default.q.15day_n3-t32-q2.explanation: Based on the sentence in the passage, 「桜が咲くと、公園などの桜の木の下で、お弁当を食べたりお酒を飲んだりする「お花見」が（　2　）。」, the completed answer 「行われます」 means: “When the cherry blossoms bloom, hanami—eating boxed lunches and drinking alcohol under cherry trees in places such as parks—is held.” Grammatically, 「行われる」 is the passive form (受身形) of the transitive verb 「行う」 (to conduct, hold). It has an objective tone and is commonly used in the pattern 「[Event/Custom] + が行われる」 when the specific people carrying it out do not need to be emphasized. Learners may hesitate over choice (a), 「行います」, so focus on the particle: when people are the organizers, use 「（人が）イベントを行う」 with 「を」; when the event is the subject marked by 「が」, as in 「お花見が」, the passive 「行われる」 is required. Also, do not confuse it with (d), 「行かれます」, which comes from the verb 「行く」 (to go) and is unrelated to the verb meaning “to hold.”

The adverb「徐々に」describes a process of change or accumulation that proceeds gradually over time and is equivalent in meaning to「少しずつ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t17-q9.explanation: The adverb 「徐々に」(じょじょに) usually precedes a verb describing a gradual process of change or learning. It has a relatively formal tone and describes something progressing slowly and step by step. The sentence 「徐々に仕事を覚えるつもりだ」means: “I intend to learn the job little by little.” For example: 「薬を飲んだら、痛みが徐々に和らいできた。」(After taking the medicine, the pain gradually began to ease.) Unlike 「いつのまにか」, which emphasizes an unnoticed change, 「徐々に」 focuses on gradual progress and is essentially equivalent to 「少しずつ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t17-q9.why.0: ✗ (a) 「いつのまにか」 means “without realizing when,” describing something that has happened without the person noticing the point at which it occurred; it does not indicate gradual progress.
default.q.15day_n3-t17-q9.why.1: ✗ (b) 「急に」means “suddenly” or “unexpectedly,” expressing a rapid change and directly contrasting with the gradual progression indicated by「徐々に」.
default.q.15day_n3-t17-q9.why.2: ✗ (c) 「あとで」means "afterward" or "later" and locates the time of a subsequent event; it does not modify degree or progression.
default.q.15day_n3-t17-q9.why.3: ✓ (d) 「少しずつ」 means “little by little” or “gradually.” It describes an action progressing step by step over time and is synonymous with 「徐々に」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 髪を切ったんですか。よく（似合って）いますね。
The verb 似合う expresses aesthetic suitability or harmony between a person’s appearance and something such as a hairstyle or outfit, making it the correct compliment for the new haircut.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q1.explanation: The verb 似合う（にあう）commonly appears in「Aは Bに 似合う／似合っている」and evaluates visual or aesthetic harmony between clothing, a hairstyle, or an accessory and someone’s appearance. In sentence (d), the speaker notices a change and naturally compliments the person: "Did you just get your hair cut? This style really suits you!" Another example is:「その着物、彼女によく似合っている。」(That kimono looks very good on her.) To avoid the trap in sentence (c), remember that 合う refers to physical fit or compatibility, such as shoe size or clothing measurements, whereas 似合う necessarily involves appearance, style, or aesthetics.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) To express similarity in speech, gestures, or personality to someone, Japanese uses the verb 似る (as in 似てきた), not 似合う.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) When talking about meeting a friend after many years, the correct verb is 会う (会った) or 出会う, not 似合う.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) When saying whether footwear fits a person's feet in size, the verb 合う (合わない) must be used, not 似合う.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q1.why.3: ✓ (d) 似合う is correctly used to praise a new hairstyle as harmonious, attractive, and well suited to the other person's appearance.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q10.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 留学を（希望）する理由を聞かせていただけますか。
「希望」 means a desire or aspiration and commonly appears in 「〜を希望する」 to express an official wish regarding study or work.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q10.explanation: 「希望」（きぼう） is a noun and a する-verb (〜を希望する) meaning "hope, wish, or aspiration." It is commonly used in formal contexts such as applications, résumés, and interviews for jobs or study abroad. Unlike everyday expressions of personal desire such as 「〜たい」 or 「欲しい」, it sounds polite and serious and suggests a clearly defined goal. The sentence means: "Could you please tell me why you wish to study abroad?" For example: 「面接でこの会社への就職を希望する理由を話しました。」 (I explained in the interview why I hoped to join this company). Use 「希望」 for a formal personal aspiration, 「期待」 for expectations of another person, 「予定」 for a plan or schedule, and 「注文」 when ordering food or drinks.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q10.why.0: ✗ (a) When ordering a drink or dish at a restaurant, Japanese uses the verb 「注文する」, not 「希望する」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q10.why.1: ✗ (b) For a schedule or plan to travel with friends, the appropriate word is 「予定」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q10.why.2: ✗ (c) To express expecting or hoping that someone will do something, use「期待している」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q10.why.3: ✓ (d) 「留学を希望する」 is a natural and correct phrase for expressing a desire to study abroad.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) あのパソコンは、（勝手）に使ってはいけません。使うときは許可を得てください。
The adverb 「勝手に」 means doing something on one's own initiative or without permission, fitting the prohibition and the following condition that permission must be obtained, 「許可を得る」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q2.explanation: 「勝手」(しょうてん) is a very common na-adjective on the JLPT N3 and is often used adverbially as 「勝手に + verb」. It means doing something as one pleases, without asking for permission or considering others, and often carries a critical nuance. The complete sentence means: "Do not use that computer without permission; please ask first before using it." Compare: 「人の日記を勝手に読まないでください。」(Please do not read someone else's diary without permission.) Do not let 「勝」mislead you into thinking of victory, as in 「優勝した」, and do not confuse standalone 「勝手」with the compound noun 「使い勝手」(a thing's ease of use).
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q2.why.0: ✓ (a) 「勝手に」means “without permission, on one’s own authority,” and fits perfectly with the prohibition「使ってはいけません」and the subsequent request「許可を得てください」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) A sentence about an athlete competing in a sporting event requires a word indicating victory, such as「優勝した」(won the championship), not「勝手」(the test writer is deliberately setting a kanji trap with「勝」).
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) To describe a store's products, adjectives such as 「人気な」(popular) or 「便利な」(convenient) are needed. 「勝手」cannot stand alone to praise or modify a product.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) When praising someone’s specialty or cooking skills, use 「得意」 (good at, one’s forte) or 「上手」, not 「勝手」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 私の国では冬はマイナス２０度になるので、日本の寒さは（平気）です。
「平気」(a na-adjective) means being calm or unaffected by a negative external condition. It appropriately expresses that the cold in Japan causes the speaker no difficulty or discomfort.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q3.explanation: 「平気」(a na-adjective) means "calm, unaffected, or able to endure something well." It commonly appears in forms such as 「〜は平気だ」or 「平気な顔」to describe not being negatively affected by difficulty, pain, or severe weather. The complete sentence means: "Because temperatures in my country drop as low as minus 20 degrees in winter, I can handle the cold in Japan just fine." Another example is: 「注射は少し痛いですが、私は平気です。」(The injection hurts a little, but I am fine.) To avoid confusion, remember that 「平気」requires some source of pressure or difficulty that the subject manages without trouble. This differs from the relaxed, burden-free feeling of 「気分が楽」(choice d) or the gentle, calm personality described by 「穏やか」(choice b).
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) To describe a tired or pale complexion caused by poor health, Japanese uses「顔色がよくない」, not「平気」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) 「平気」is not used as an adjective to describe a person's calm and gentle personality; words such as 「穏やか」or 「大人しい」are needed.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q3.why.2: ✓ (c) The adjective「平気」is very naturally used to express that the speaker can handle something without feeling bothered by the cold in Japan.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q3.why.3: ✗ (d) To express feeling relaxed and relieved because work is not too busy, the correct word is 「楽」(らく), not 「平気」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) あまりにびっくりしたので、（思わず）大声を出してしまった。
The adverb 「思わず」describes an involuntary action caused by a sudden stimulus, fitting the context of accidentally shouting after being startled.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q4.explanation: The adverb 「思わず」means “involuntarily” or “without being able to stop oneself.” It describes an immediate unconscious reaction that reason cannot control in time and often combines with the ending 「～てしまった」. The complete meaning of the correct sentence is: "I was so astonished that I blurted out a loud cry." Compare: 「映画のラストシーンを見て、思わず涙が出た。」 (When I saw the final scene of the movie, I could not help shedding tears.) For the JLPT, remember that 「思わず」does not combine with causative or request forms such as ～ないでください, is not used for an action continuing over a period like 「ずっと」, and should not be confused with 「うっかり」, which describes carelessness or forgetfulness.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q4.why.0: ✗ (a) 「思わず」describes an involuntary reflex and is not used with a prohibition or deliberate request such as 「～ないでください」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q4.why.1: ✓ (b) It correctly expresses letting out a cry involuntarily after being startled, naturally combining with the ending「～てしまった」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) Since the staff member deliberately brought a towel to help the customer, the action is thoughtful and considerate. 「すぐに」 or 「気を利かせて」 should be used instead of a term describing an unconscious action.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) An action continuing over a long period, marked by the adverb「ずっと」, cannot be used with the instantaneous reflexive expression「思わず」. 「ぼんやり」is appropriate instead.

✅ Correct answer: (b) 会社の（偉い）人と話す機会は、めったにない。
The adjective「偉い」is correctly used to modify「人」and refer to someone with a high position or status in an organization or society.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q5.explanation: 「偉い」 (an -i adjective) has two core meanings: describing someone with a high position, rank, or authority in an organization or society, and praising someone’s outstanding or admirable actions. In the workplace, 「偉い人」 is commonly used to refer to superiors or senior officials, so the correct sentence means: “I hardly ever get the chance to talk with the senior leaders at my company.” Another example showing the meaning “admirable” is: 「自分で学費を稼いで大学を卒業した彼は本当に偉い。」 (He worked to pay his own tuition and graduated from college; he is truly admirable.) Distinguish 「偉い」 from other words describing advantages: use 「年上」 (choice a) for an age difference, 「人気がある」 (choice c) for popularity, and 「強い」 (choice d) for physical strength or competitive ability.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q5.why.0: ✗ (a) To express an age difference, use「年上」or「年下」, not「偉い」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q5.why.1: ✓ (b) 「偉い人」is a very natural expression for someone in a high position or a company leader.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q5.why.2: ✗ (c) To express being admired or liked by many people, especially women, the phrase 「人気がある」must be used, not 「偉い」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q5.why.3: ✗ (d) To describe dominant athletic performance and repeated victories in sports, 「強い」must be used instead of 「偉い」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q6.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) この店の料理は（ボリューム）があるが、値段はそれほど高くない。
The expression 「ボリュームがある」 is commonly used to describe a large, substantial serving of food, fitting the contrast with the reasonable price.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q6.explanation: The katakana noun 「ボリューム」, borrowed from the English word “volume,” can refer not only to a device’s sound level but also to the size, richness, or quantity of a meal. In dining contexts, it commonly appears in expressions such as 「ボリュームがある」 (a generous portion) and 「ボリューム満点」 (extremely filling). Therefore, sentence (d) means: “The portions at this restaurant are very generous, yet the prices are not expensive at all.” For example: 「この定食はボリューム満点で、男性でもお腹がいっぱいになる。」 (This set meal is so generous that even a man would feel full.) To distinguish choice (c), remember that 「ボリュームを上げる/下げる」 refers only to turning a speaker, television, or other device up or down. To improve ability through practice, use 「腕を上げる」 or 「レベルが上がる」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q6.why.0: ✗ (a) When praising a phone’s sharp images or clear sound quality, the nouns「写真」or「音質」are used, rather than combining the adjective「きれいな」with「ボリューム」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q6.why.1: ✗ (b) To describe bodily growth that makes someone taller than another person, the appropriate word is「身長」(height), not「ボリューム」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q6.why.2: ✗ (c) In a context of daily training to improve or raise one’s level, words such as 「腕」 (“skill”) or 「実力」 (“ability”) are appropriate; 「ボリューム」 is not used with this meaning.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q6.why.3: ✓ (d) The expression 「ボリュームがある」 accurately describes a large, filling dish and contrasts appropriately with a price that is not too high.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q7.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) となりに住んでいる人は、（たまに）見かけるぐらいで、どんな人かわからない。
The adverb 「たまに」describes an action that occurs very infrequently, meaning “occasionally” or “once in a while.” It fits the context because the speaker only occasionally sees the neighbor and does not know what kind of person they are.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q7.explanation: 「たまに」is a frequency adverb meaning “occasionally / sometimes,” usually placed before a verb to describe something that happens very infrequently, less often than 「ときどき」. In sentence c, this usage is completely natural: “I only occasionally see the person who lives next door, so I have no idea what kind of person they are.” A typical example is: 「普段は家で料理を作りますが、たまに外のレストランで食べます。」(I usually cook at home, but occasionally I eat at a restaurant.) For the N3 test, distinguish 「たまに」(low frequency, used with an affirmative statement) from 「めったに…ない」(hardly ever, which must be used with a negative), and do not confuse it with 「たまたま」(by chance, accidentally).
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q7.why.0: ✗ (a) This sentence describes something happening after a long period without seeing someone since graduation, so an adverb such as 「久しぶりに」 is required, not a word indicating repeated frequency such as 「たまに」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q7.why.1: ✗ (b) The preceding clause presents a rare opportunity (めったにない機会), so it cannot be combined with 「たまに」 (“occasionally”). A word expressing determination or certainty, such as 「ぜひ」 or 「必ず」, is required.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q7.why.2: ✓ (c) The adverb 「たまに」 is correctly used to indicate an occasional frequency, expressing that the speaker only sometimes encounters the neighbor and therefore does not know what kind of person they are.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q7.why.3: ✗ (d) Being close to employees like friends requires visiting frequently, so 「よく」or「しょっちゅう」must be used. 「たまに」creates a logical contradiction.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q8.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) この機械はまるで人の手のように、動きが（スムーズ）ですね。
The word 「スムーズ」, from the English word “smooth,” means flowing, smooth, or trouble-free. It is appropriate for describing a machine’s movement as smooth and uninterrupted.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q8.explanation: 「スムーズ」is a na-adjective, commonly used as 「スムーズだ／な／に」. Borrowed from the English word “smooth,” it describes a process, event, or movement that proceeds smoothly and continuously without problems or interruption. In choice (d), 「動きがスムーズ」appropriately describes the machine’s fluid movement. The complete sentence means: "This machine’s movement is so smooth and graceful, just like a person’s hand, isn’t it?" It also commonly combines with verbs describing work progress or traffic, as in: 「先輩の助けがあったので、プロジェクトがスムーズに進みました。」(Thanks to my senior colleague’s help, the project progressed smoothly.) Do not confuse it with choice (c). When describing convenience in daily life, use the adjective 「便利」; 「スムーズ」emphasizes uninterrupted flow or movement.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q8.why.0: ✗ (a) To describe drinking in one gulp or gulping down beer when thirsty, expressions such as「一気に」or「ごくごくと」are used, not「スムーズ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q8.why.1: ✗ (b) To describe comfortable, casual clothing for getting together with friends, the appropriate word is 「カジュアル」or 「楽」, not 「スムーズ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q8.why.2: ✗ (c) To describe a room or residence as convenient because it is near a supermarket and convenience store, the na-adjective「便利」must be used, not「スムーズ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q8.why.3: ✓ (d) 「スムーズ」is correctly used to describe a machine’s movement (動き) as smooth and unobstructed.

✅ Correct answer: (b) 庭の草花の（世話をする）のは、父の担当だ。
The phrase「世話をする」means to take care of or look after people, animals, or plants, making it appropriate for caring for the flowers and plants in the garden.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q9.explanation: The expression「〜の世話をする」(usually following a noun referring to the person or thing requiring care, with the particle の) means to care for, look after, or attend to. It is used for living things that require attention, such as children, sick people, pets, or plants. The complete sentence (b) means: "My father is responsible for taking care of the flowers and plants in the garden." For this usage, consider:「母が入院している間、妹の世話をした。」(I looked after my younger sister while my mother was in the hospital.) In test questions, remember that「世話をする」refers to practical daily care, not conversational interaction (as in choices a and c, which use「相談する」/「話す」) or scolding and discipline (as in choice d, which uses「叱る」).
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q9.why.0: ✗ (a) When troubled and wanting to confide in friends or ask for advice, the verb「相談する」(to discuss or seek advice) must be used, not「世話をする」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q9.why.1: ✓ (b) The expression 「草花の世話をする」correctly describes watering, fertilizing, and caring for flowers and plants in a garden。
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q9.why.2: ✗ (c) To talk about chatting with friends on the phone, the correct verb is 「話す」or 「おしゃべりする」, not 「世話をする」.
default.q.15day_n3-t18-q9.why.3: ✗ (d) After making a serious mistake and being reprimanded by a superior, the passive form of 「叱る」, 「叱られた」 (“was scolded”), is required, not 「世話をされた」.
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) これからカレーの（材料）を買いに行くところだ。
The noun 「材料」(ざいりょう) means ingredients or materials used to make something, making it exactly suitable for the food used to prepare curry.
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q1.explanation: The noun 「材料」(ざいりょう) refers to the specific ingredients or components that make up a product, especially food, handicrafts, or manufactured goods. It commonly appears in the structure 「[finished product] + の材料」. In context, the sentence means: “I’m about to go out and buy the ingredients for curry.” Another example is 「ケーキを作るために、スーパーで材料をそろえた。」 (I bought all the ingredients at the supermarket to make a cake.) At N3 level, watch for the classic confusion between 「材料」 (tangible ingredients or materials) and 「資料」(しりょう) (documents or data used in meetings or research).
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) To express preparing one’s own food or lunch box each day, Japanese uses「弁当」(lunch box) or「料理」(dish/food), not「材料」.
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) Printed documents and informational materials distributed at a meeting are called「資料」(しりょう, materials/documents), not「材料」.
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) When referring to the technical features or functions of a camera device, the correct word is 「機能」(きのう)。
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q1.why.3: ✓ (d) 「材料」 combines correctly with 「カレー」 in the phrase 「カレーの材料」, meaning the food ingredients used to make curry。
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q10.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) あの日は（たしか）家族で水族館に行ったと思います。
The adverb 「たしか」means “if I remember correctly” or “I believe,” expressing a guess based on the speaker’s uncertain memory, so it fits well with the predicate 「～と思います」.
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q10.explanation: The adverb 「たしか」(確か) is used when the speaker relies on personal memory but is not completely certain, with the nuance "if I remember correctly" or "I think...". It therefore often appears with structures expressing supposition or recollection, such as 「～と思う」and 「～はずだ」. In context (b), the complete sentence means: "If I remember correctly, my whole family went to the aquarium that day." A similar example is:「田中さんの誕生日は、たしか来週だったと思います。」(If I remember correctly, Mr. Tanaka's birthday is next week.) For the JLPT, distinguish 「たしか」(a tentative recollection) from 「たしかに」(indeed, certainly, confirming an obvious fact or agreeing with someone) and 「正確に」(accurately).
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q10.why.0: ✗ (a) When asking someone to fill in information accurately and clearly, an adverb such as 「正確に」or 「ちゃんと」must be used, not 「たしか」.
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q10.why.1: ✓ (b) 「たしか」combines naturally with the conjectural ending「～と思います」to express a past memory that the speaker is no longer completely certain about.
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q10.why.2: ✗ (c) In advice or a request to choose an object one likes, an adverb expressing a guess about memory cannot be used; a quantity word such as「ひとつ」is needed.
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q10.why.3: ✗ (d) To announce that one is preparing to leave or to ask permission to leave, time-related adverbs such as「もう」or「そろそろ」are used, not「たしか」.
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 銀行でお金を３万円（おろした）。
The verb 「おろす」 (下ろす) combines with 「お金」 to mean withdrawing money from an account or bank.
default.q.15day_n3-t19-q2.explanation: In N3 Japanese, the Group 1 transitive verb「おろす」, written「下ろす」, is commonly used to mean withdrawing money from a bank or account in the phrase「（銀行・口座から）お金をおろす」. The complete sentence in the correct answer means: "I went to the bank and withdrew 30,000 yen in cash." Similar example:「急な出費があったので、コンビニのATMでお金をおろしました。」(I had an unexpected expense, so I withdrew money from a convenience-store ATM.) To avoid confusion, remember: lowering the temperature or volume uses「下げる」(さげる), passengers getting off a train or vehicle use the intransitive verb「降りる」(おりる), and removing stains uses the fixed expression「汚れを落とす」(おとす).

To distinguish related terms: 「見物」 is for entertainment and sightseeing, such as viewing flowers or fireworks; 「見学」 is visiting to learn through observation, such as at a club or factory; and 「鑑賞」 is appreciating works of art or music. The expression「素直に言う」describes expressing one's feelings or wishes honestly and straightforwardly, without hiding them or hesitating.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q6.explanation: 「素直」（すなお）is a na-adjective with two main meanings: obedient and willing to listen, or honest and straightforward about one's true feelings when used adverbially as 「素直に + verb」. In choice (c), the sentence means: "If you really want to go, just be honest and say that you want to go." Example: 「彼は自分の非を素直に認めた。」(He honestly admitted his fault.) An important distinction is that the kanji 「直」in 「素直」can make learners associate it with "straight" (まっすぐ, as in choice d) or "simple" (choice b), but this word describes a person's character or attitude.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q6.why.0: ✗ (a) When warning someone not to touch something dangerous, words such as 「むやみに」 or 「絶対に」 are commonly used, not 「素直に」.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q6.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because the appropriate words for describing a simple, plain design contrasted with something flashy (派手) are 「シンプルな」 or 「地味な」; 「素直」is not used for the design of an object.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q6.why.2: ✓ (c) 「素直に言う」expresses honestly revealing one's feelings and wishes without hesitation or beating around the bush.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q6.why.3: ✗ (d) To indicate going straight along a road, Japanese uses the directional adverb「まっすぐ」;「素直」is not used for physical space.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q7.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 最近買ったテレビの使い方について、（問い合わせ）の電話をした。
The noun 「問い合わせ」, from 「問い合わせる」, is commonly used when a customer or individual contacts a company, institution, or support center to ask for information or clarification about a product or service.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q7.explanation: The verb「問い合わせる」(with the noun「問い合わせ」; common patterns include「〜について問い合わせる」and「〜にお問い合わせください」) is formal and means to contact an organization, company, office, or shop to obtain detailed information or ask about a product, service, or administrative procedure. Sentence (b) means: “I called to ask how to use the television I recently bought.” Example:「ご不明な点がございましたら、サポートセンターまでお問い合わせください。」(If you have any questions, please contact the support center.) The key distinction is that「問い合わせる」is used for contacting an organization or service. Use「質問する」for asking about homework or professional matters, and「聞く」or「尋ねる」for everyday questions to acquaintances or strangers.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q7.why.0: ✗ (a) When asking a teacher to explain an unclear lesson again, use 「質問する」 or 「聞く」, not 「問い合わせる」.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q7.why.1: ✓ (b) The noun phrase 「問い合わせの電話」 accurately describes calling the support desk to ask how to operate the television.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q7.why.2: ✗ (c) When lost and asking a passerby for directions, Japanese speakers use 「道を聞く」or 「尋ねる」, not 「問い合わせる」.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q7.why.3: ✗ (d) When discussing household matters such as one's schedule with a family member like one's mother, the ordinary verb 「聞く」is used; 「問い合わせる」would sound stiff and inappropriate.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q8.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 急に予定が入ってしまったので、来週の旅行は（キャンセル）することになった。
「キャンセル」means to cancel a schedule or plan that had already been arranged. It fits the context of canceling the trip.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q8.explanation: The word 「キャンセル」 (from English “cancel”) combines with 「する」 to form a verb meaning to cancel a confirmed appointment, agreement, or reservation, such as a ticket, hotel room, or tour. Sentence (a) means: “Because something urgent suddenly came up, I had to cancel next week’s trip.” Another example is:「体調を崩したので、歯医者の予約をキャンセルした。」(I canceled my dentist appointment because I became ill.) Remember that 「キャンセル」 applies to canceling an arrangement or plan. It cannot replace verbs meaning to quit a job (辞める), reduce something (減らす), or complete or discontinue one’s studies (卒業/中退), as in choices (b), (c), and (d).
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q8.why.0: ✓ (a) The expression 「キャンセルする」is correctly used to describe canceling a prearranged trip or schedule.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q8.why.1: ✗ (b) When finishing a period of work or quitting a job at a store, 「終わり」or 「辞める」must be used, not 「キャンセル」.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q8.why.2: ✗ (c) When reducing the amount of training by half, the appropriate word is「減らした」or「短縮した」, not「キャンセル」.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q8.why.3: ✗ (d) When someone completes university, Japanese uses「卒業」(graduation), or「中退」if they leave school partway through, not「キャンセル」.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q9.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) （期限）までに必ず書類を出してください。
「期限」means the deadline for completing a task or procedure and correctly combines with 「〜までに」, meaning that the documents must be submitted by that time.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q9.explanation: The noun 「期限」（きげん）refers to the final time by which an obligation or task must be completed. It has a binding nuance and commonly appears in submission contexts with 「期限までに」. The complete sentence means: "You must submit all the documents before the deadline." Example: 「レポートの提出期限は明日の午後５時です。」(The deadline for submitting the report is 5:00 p.m. tomorrow.) For the N3 exam, distinguish 「期限」(deadline), 「期間」(a duration with a beginning and end), and 「時期」(a time or season suitable for something).
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q9.why.0: ✓ (a) The noun「期限」means a term or deadline, and combining it with the particle「までに」creates a completely natural expression when requesting that an application be submitted.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q9.why.1: ✗ (b) When referring to the date and time of an event such as a wedding, Japanese uses 「日程」or「日時」, not「期限」.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q9.why.2: ✗ (c) A construction-site context requires a word indicating a period of time, such as「期間」or「間」; the deadline word「期限」cannot be used.
default.q.15day_n3-t20-q9.why.3: ✗ (d) This sentence describes the appropriate time of year for viewing flowers, so the correct word to fill the blank is「時期」.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) うえに
The pattern 「〜うえに」means “not only... but also...” and links two negative circumstances in the same direction: working overtime continuously and having to work weekends, resulting in exhaustion.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q1.explanation: The grammar pattern 「Plain form + 上に（うえに）」—with na-adjectives retaining な and nouns taking の—means “not only ... but also ...” and adds another fact or state with the same evaluative direction as the first, either positive or negative. In the test sentence, the complete meaning is: “Last week, not only did my overtime continue for an extended period, but I also had to work on the weekend, so my body was completely exhausted.” Another example is:「このアパートは家賃が安いうえに、駅からも近くて便利だ」(This apartment is not only inexpensive but also conveniently close to the station.) Do not confuse 「うえに」 with the adverb 「さらに」 (choice (d) is tempting because both mean “furthermore”). 「さらに」 is an independent adverb placed at the beginning of a sentence or before the predicate, whereas 「うえに」 is a dependent connective that follows the plain form of a verb and links two clauses.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜ままに」 means “as is” or “in accordance with,” and is not suitable for expressing two events accumulating together.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q1.why.1: ✓ (b) 「〜うえに」 combines with the plain form (続いた) to mean “not only... but also...,” adding weekend work to the burden of continuous overtime.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜ために」indicates a cause-and-effect relationship or purpose, so it is inappropriate because working on weekends is not a direct result of working overtime.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) 「さらに」 is an independent adverb that usually appears at the beginning of a sentence; it cannot directly follow the plain-form verb 「続いた」 to link two clauses.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q10.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) だっけ
The structure「だっけ」follows a noun in informal speech to confirm information the speaker once knew but cannot clearly remember now.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q10.explanation: In casual conversation, 「～っけ / ～だっけ」often follows the plain past form, especially with nouns or na-adjectives using 「だ / だった」, to show that the speaker is trying to remember or confirm something they once knew but are not currently sure about. Applied to the exam sentence, the complete dialogue is: A: “Mr. Kawamoto is from Kyoto, right?” B: “Yes, that’s right.” A similar situation is asking about a schedule: 「明日の会議は何時からだっけ。」(What time does tomorrow’s meeting start again?). To avoid distractors, remember that 「だっけ」is used to ask about one’s memory, unlike 「だけ」(only; a limited quantity) and the suffix 「～たて」(added to the verb stem to describe something that has just been completed).
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q10.why.0: ✗ (a) The suffix「たて」follows the ます-stem of a verb to express that something has just been completed; it does not follow a noun directly.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q10.why.1: ✗ (b) The structure 「たって」 is the spoken form of 「ても」 (“even if”), and is not used as a sentence ending to ask for confirmation.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q10.why.2: ✓ (c) The sentence ending 「だっけ」combines directly with the noun 「京都出身」to ask for confirmation about something the speaker does not clearly remember.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q10.why.3: ✗ (d) The particle 「だけ」expresses limitation (“only”); it does not function as an interrogative marker for recalling or confirming something.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q11.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) させられる
The causative-passive form 考えさせられる expresses how a work of art or an objective event affects viewers and naturally makes them think deeply about their own lives.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q11.explanation: In N3 grammar, the causative-passive form (使役受身) of the Group II verb 考える is 考えさせられる. It is often used with verbs of thought or perception to express being prompted by an external event to think about something. The complete sentence means: “This film is a work that makes viewers reflect on their own lives.” Compare: 「子供の素朴な質問に、深く考えさせられた。」(The child’s innocent question made me think deeply.) Do not confuse it with choice (b) される. The simple passive 考えられる is used for an objective judgment such as “is considered,” whereas 考えさせられる expresses a personal response in which outside circumstances compel someone to reflect.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q11.why.0: ✓ (a) The causative-passive form 考えさせられる accurately expresses being deeply affected by the film and made to reflect on life.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q11.why.1: ✗ (b) The ordinary passive form される means “be thought of” or indicates possibility, but it cannot express being prompted by external circumstances to start thinking.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q11.why.2: ✗ (c) The causative-passive form of 考え付く (“come up with an idea”) would be 付かされる, which is both semantically incorrect and unnatural in this context of reflecting on life.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q11.why.3: ✗ (d) The passive form 付かれる of 考え付く (to come up with an idea) is completely inappropriate for the meaning of deeply reflecting on life.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q12.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) おいた
The pattern「〜ておく」(past form:「〜ておいた」) indicates deliberately doing something in advance to prepare for a future event or situation.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q12.explanation: The key pattern is 「Verb te-form + おく」, which becomes 「〜ておいた」 in the past. It describes deliberately completing an action in advance as preparation for a later task or event. The complete sentence means: “Since I will be busy with meetings all day tomorrow, I finished the proposal in advance today.” A similar example is: 「パーティーの前に、飲み物をたくさん買っておいた。」(Before the party, I bought plenty of drinks in advance.) To distinguish it from choice (c), 「〜てあった」, remember that 「〜ておく」 focuses on the subject’s preparatory action and takes an object marked by を (企画書を作っておく), whereas 「〜てあった」 emphasizes the resulting state of an object, which commonly appears with が (企画書が作ってある).
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q12.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜ていた」 indicates an action in progress in the past or a continuing state; it does not express the purpose of making preparations in advance.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q12.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜ていった」indicates movement away from the speaker or a gradual change over time, so its meaning is completely inappropriate here.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q12.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜てあった」 describes a state remaining after someone has performed an action (usually with が, as in 企画書が〜), and is not used to describe preparing something oneself.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q12.why.3: ✓ (d) 「〜ておいた」(the past form of 〜ておく) combines with 作る in the te-form to create 「作っておいた」, expressing that the plan was prepared in advance for a busy day tomorrow.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q13.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) まで
The particle まで combines with a noun to emphasize that an unexpected event extends even to the least expected person or thing, meaning “even” or “to the extent of.”
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q13.explanation: In N3 grammar, noun + まで introduces an extreme or unusual example to emphasize the degree of something, expressing surprise or regret with the meaning 'even' or 'as far as'. Here, the speaker is surprised and apologetic that a mistake they themselves made also caused unrelated colleague Kimura to be reprimanded. The complete sentence means: "Although I was the one who made the mistake, even my colleague Kimura was reprimanded by the manager." A similar example is: 「親友にまで疑われるなんて、本当にショックだ。」(It is truly shocking to be suspected even by my best friend.) Do not confuse まで (emphasis: 'even') with までに (a deadline by which something must be completed) or うえに (addition: 'in addition' or 'not only... but also').
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q13.why.0: ✗ (a) うえ is a noun meaning “above” or used in the pattern 「〜た上で」 (“after doing”), and it cannot follow a noun referring to a person to express involvement or consequences.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q13.why.1: ✗ (b) うえに is a grammar pattern meaning “not only... but also...” and adds information in the same direction. It does not fit this unexpected situation in which someone else is scolded as well.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q13.why.2: ✓ (c) まで follows a noun to indicate that something extends to an extreme or unexpected target, meaning “even” or “as far as.”
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q13.why.3: ✗ (d) までに is a particle marking a deadline by which an action must be completed (“by,” “no later than”), so it is semantically incorrect in this sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q14.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) たまらない
The structure 「～てたまらない」 follows the て-form of an adjective expressing desire (ほしくて) and describes an overwhelming longing that cannot be restrained.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q14.explanation: The N3 pattern「～てたまらない」combines with i-adjectives (remove い and add くて), na-adjectives (add で), or verbs in the te-form. It expresses an intense, uncontrollable emotion, physical sensation, or desire arising naturally, meaning “extremely...” or “cannot stand...” In the test context, 「新しく発売された携帯電話がほしくてたまらない」means: “I desperately want the newly released mobile phone.” Because the blank follows「ほしくて」in the te-form, only「たまらない」fits grammatically. Choices such as「違いない」and「しかない」must follow the plain form or dictionary form. Another typical example is: 「合格の知らせを聞いて、嬉しくてたまらなかった」(I was overjoyed when I heard that I had passed.)
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q14.why.0: ✗ (a) 「～に違いない」expresses a confident judgment (“must be”) and must directly follow the plain form (ほしい). It cannot follow the て-form (ほしくて).
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q14.why.1: ✓ (b) 「～てたまらない」combines perfectly with the te-form of an adjective expressing desire (ほしくて) to emphasize an overwhelming, uncontrollable feeling: “want very badly.”
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q14.why.2: ✗ (c) 「～ことはない」means “there is no need to do something” and combines with the dictionary form of a verb. It is inappropriate both structurally and semantically here.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q14.why.3: ✗ (d)「～しかない」means “there is no choice but to...” and is followed by a dictionary-form verb or a noun, not an adjective in the te-form.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q15.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) なり
Before the particle 「に」, the verb 「なる」can form 火事になる. Before 「かねず」, the verb must be in the ます-stem form, giving なり.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q15.explanation: The key pattern is「V-ます stem + かねない / かねず」, expressing concern that something negative or dangerous is quite likely to happen if careless behavior continues. The complete sentence means: “Even if you think you have put it out, throwing a cigarette butt into a trash can could still cause a fire, which is extremely dangerous.” The key to avoiding confusion between「なる」and「起きる」is the particle「に」: Japanese says「火事になる」, not「火事に起きる」(though「火事が起きる」is possible). Since the pattern requires the V-ます stem, the correct form is「なり」rather than the dictionary form「なる」. For comparison:「無理な運転を続けると、事故を起こしかねない」(If you keep driving recklessly, you could easily cause an accident.)
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q15.why.0: ✗ (a) Although 起き is in the V-ます stem form, the particle is incorrect: the verb 起きる takes が (火事が起きる), not に.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q15.why.1: ✗ (b) 起きる is incorrect both in particle usage (it should be 火事が起きる) and in the grammatical form required before かねず (the V-ます form with ます removed).
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q15.why.2: ✓ (c) なり is the ます-stem of the verb なる, satisfying the grammar rule before かねず while also forming the natural phrase 火事になる.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q15.why.3: ✗ (d) なるcombines appropriately with the particle に, but its conjugation is incorrect because the V-ます stem must be used before かねず.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) かけ
The suffix かけ attaches to the verb stem after removing ます and expresses an unfinished action in progress. 「作りかけの資料」 (“documents still being prepared”) is grammatically and semantically correct.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q2.explanation: The pattern 「～かけ」combines with the V-ます stem to describe an action that has begun but has been interrupted before completion. It is often used before a noun in the form [V-stem + かけの + N] to describe something unfinished. In the question, the complete sentence means: “Through carelessness, I accidentally deleted some data from the document I was still working on.” A common example to remember it by is: 「テーブルの上に飲みかけのコーヒーがある。」(There is a half-finished cup of coffee on the table.) To distinguish it from 「最中」, note that 「～かけ」focuses on the unfinished nature of an object or task and attaches directly to the verb stem, whereas 「最中」emphasizes the point when an action is in progress and must be used with 「V-ている」or 「Nの」.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q2.why.0: ✓ (a) Attaching it to the verb stem formed by removing ます creates the noun phrase 「作りかけの資料」, describing unfinished materials that are still being prepared.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) ながら expresses two actions occurring simultaneously, and there is no structure [V-stem + ながら + の + N] for modifying a noun.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) 最中 requires the structure [V-ている最中] or [Nの最中] to indicate that something is in the middle of happening; it cannot follow the verb stem 作り directly.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) The noun 際means “when” or “on the occasion of” and must be combined with the dictionary form, た-form, or [N + の]; this is incorrect in both structure and context.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) しては
The pattern 「N + にしては」expresses surprise when reality—here, a low temperature—contrasts with what is normally expected for a specific point in time, such as August in summer.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q3.explanation: The pattern「N + にしては」(or plain form + にしては; な-adjectives and nouns do not take だ) expresses an evaluation or surprise when reality differs significantly from what is normally expected of a person, thing, or specific point in time. In the test context, the complete sentence means: “Although it is August, in the middle of summer, today’s temperature is fairly low.” Learners often confuse「にしては」with「わりに」, but the combination is different:「にしては」directly follows a noun (Nにしては), whereas「わりに」requires の after a noun (Nのわりに), never「Nにわりに」. Example:「この子は5歳にしては、ずいぶん敬語を上手に使う。」(Although this child is only five, they use honorific language remarkably well.)
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) With a noun, the grammar pattern 「わりに」must use 「N + のわりに」; it cannot be combined with 「Nに」.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) 「からといって」(even if one says that...) must be combined with the plain form; with a noun, 「だ」must be added, and the following clause generally uses a partially negative structure.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜に反して」(contrary to...) combines with nouns expressing predictions, expectations, or rules, such as 予想, 期待, or 規則. It does not combine with a natural time reference.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q3.why.3: ✓ (d) Correct because 「N + にしては」combines directly with a noun indicating a time reference to describe something contrary to the usual impression of August, namely the low temperature.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) した
The pattern「Vた + ばかり」describes an action that has just been completed from the speaker’s perspective, so 開店する must take the past form した.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q4.explanation: The grammar pattern「Vた + ばかり」combines the short past form with「ばかり」to describe an action that ended only a short time ago, based on the speaker’s subjective perception. The adverb「さっき」(just now) signals a very recent event, so 開店する must become「開店した」. The complete sentence means: "This bakery is extremely popular—even though it only opened a little while ago, some items have already sold out." Distinguish this from「Vる + ばかり」, which can express the complaint that someone does nothing but something or the idea that something remains to be done. It is not used for a completed action. Example:「日本に来たばかりの頃は、道に迷ってばかりいました。」(When I had just arrived in Japan, I was constantly getting lost.)
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q4.why.0: ✓ (a) Correct because the pattern「Vた + ばかり」combines with the short past form (Vた) to indicate that an action has just been completed.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because the 「Vて」 form does not combine with 「ばかり」 to create a pattern expressing that an action has just occurred.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) This is incorrect because the dictionary-form pattern 「Vる + ばかり」 means “do nothing but...” or “be just about to do...,” which does not fit the context of a shop having opened.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) Incorrect because the progressive form 「Vている」 cannot combine with 「ばかり」 to express that something has just happened.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q5.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) よって
Following the noun 「曜日」(day of the week), the structure 「〜によって」means “depending on” or “according to,” accurately expressing that the menu changes by day.
default.q.15day_n3-t21-q5.explanation: The key pattern「noun + によって」indicates the basis or standard according to which the situation or state in the following clause differs or changes. It commonly occurs with words such as「変わる」,「違う」, and「様々」. The complete sentence means: “At my company cafeteria, the menu changes depending on the day of the week.” The easily confused choice (b),「〜につれて」, expresses a parallel progression in which a change in A causes a change in B. When different cases or people correspond to different results, use「〜によって」. A common example is:「人によって考え方が違います。」(People’s ways of thinking differ depending on the person.)
