default.q.15day_n3-t22-q5.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) あるんじゃない
The pattern 「～んじゃない？」with a rising intonation at the end expresses a tentative judgment or gentle suggestion that something may happen in the situation.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q5.explanation: The pattern 「plain form + んじゃない？」, with な added for na-adjectives and nouns, is the conversational contraction of 「～のではないか」. With rising intonation at the end, it presents a tentative guess or suggestion to the listener, meaning “could it be...?” or “isn’t it...?” In the dialogue, the complete meaning is: A: “Oh no, I can’t find my wallet!” B: “Could it be in your bag?” Another example is: 「田中さんはもう帰ったんじゃない？」(Isn’t Mr. Tanaka already home?) Distinguish it from option (a), 「あるわけない」, which expresses an absolute denial based on certainty (“There’s no way it exists”). The question mark and the context of looking for an item require B to make an open-ended guess that helps the listener recall where it might be.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q5.why.0: ✗ (a) The pattern 「～わけがない」asserts that something is absolutely impossible, which is the opposite of suggesting where to look for an item.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q5.why.1: ✓ (b) The phrase「～んじゃない？」expresses a gentle conjecture or suggestion, making it natural when suggesting that the other person check their bag again.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q5.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern 「～といい」expresses a wish or blessing, so it is not appropriate for guessing the location of an object.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q5.why.3: ✗ (d) The pattern 「～とする」sets up an assumption for an argument; it is not used for an ordinary speculative question.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q6.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) しか
In Japanese, the structure 「V-る + しかない」means that there is no choice but to do the stated action, which fits the situation of having missed the bus and therefore having to take a taxi.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q6.explanation: The key grammar pattern is「V-る (dictionary form) + しかない」. It is used when the speaker is stuck and has no viable option except to perform that action, conveying reluctant acceptance of the situation. Because the speaker missed the bus, the complete sentence is: "Since I missed the bus, I have no choice but to take a taxi." Compare:「終電が終わってしまったので、歩いて帰るしかない。」(The last train has already finished, so I have no choice but to walk home.) Do not confuse it with「～までもない」, which means that something is not necessary or not worth doing because it is too simple or obvious—essentially the opposite of「しかない」.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q6.why.0: ✗ (a) The pattern 「～までもない」 means that there is no need to do something, which is the exact opposite of a context requiring an alternative means of transportation after missing the vehicle.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q6.why.1: ✗ (b) The expression 「行くもない」 is grammatically incorrect, and this pattern does not exist in Japanese.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q6.why.2: ✗ (c) 「～までない」is not a standard grammar pattern that can be inserted into the sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q6.why.3: ✓ (d) The structure 「V-る + しかない」is the correct answer and means that one has no choice but to do something.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q7.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) にわたって
The grammar pattern 「〜にわたって」 follows a noun indicating an amount or range, here 200 meters, and expresses that something extends across the entire space.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q7.explanation: The structure 「Noun indicating time, space, or quantity + にわたって」 describes a large-scale state, action, or phenomenon that extends across an entire spatial range or continues throughout a period of time. The complete sentence means: “Cherry trees have been planted all along the 200 meters from this bridge to the bridge on the other side.” A familiar time-related example is: 「会議は５時間にわたって行われました。」(The meeting continued for five hours.) To distinguish it from 「〜において」, which simply indicates a static location or setting, remember that 「〜にわたって」 is used when the preceding expression is a specific distance or duration, such as メートル, キロ, 日間, or 年間.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q7.why.0: ✗ (a) The structure 「〜にとって」means “for” or “from the perspective of.” It cannot be used directly with a quantity indicating distance or length.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q7.why.1: ✓ (b) The pattern 「〜にわたって」correctly combines with a distance quantity (２００メートル) to express cherry trees planted continuously along that entire distance.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q7.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜において」is used to specify the place or field in which something occurs (“at” or “in”). It does not express extension across a spatial distance.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q7.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜に比べて」is used to contrast or compare things ('compared with...'), so it does not fit the context of the sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q8.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 以来
The pattern 「N + 以来」 describes a state that has continued from a past event up to the present.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q8.explanation: The grammar pattern 「N / V-て + 以来（いらい）」is combined with a noun referring to a past event or a verb in the te-form. It means that since the event occurred, a new state has continued up to the present. Thus, 「去年の事故以来、車の運転はしていません」means: “I have not driven a car since the accident last year.” Similar example: 「日本へ来て以来、毎朝ジョギングを続けています」(I have continued jogging every morning since I came to Japan.) Remember the distinction: 「際に」refers to a specific occasion, 「たびに」describes a repeated action (“every time”), and 「以来」requires the following state to continue over time.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q8.why.0: ✗ (a) 「ばかり」means “only,” “nothing but,” or “just,” so it is completely unsuitable in meaning and structure in this context.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q8.why.1: ✗ (b) 「たびに」 means “every time/whenever” and describes repeated events, so it cannot be used with a single event such as last year’s accident.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q8.why.2: ✓ (c) 「以来」combines with a noun marking an event in the past to mean “ever since,” which fits the continuing state expressed in the following clause.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q8.why.3: ✗ (d) 「際に」 means “when” or “on the occasion of,” and is used for the time when an action occurs. It does not express a state continuing from the past to the present.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q9.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) うちに
The structure 「〜うちに」 expresses the intention to take advantage of the current state and do something before it changes.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q9.explanation: The grammar pattern 「V-dictionary form / V-ている / V-ない / A-い / A-な / N-の + うちに」 is used when the speaker wants to take the opportunity to do something intentionally before favorable circumstances or conditions pass. Applied to the question, the completed sentence expresses the desire: “While I am still staying in Japan, I would really like to explore Hokkaido at least once.” A similar everyday example is: 「スープが温かいうちに、どうぞ飲んでください。」(Please drink the soup while it is still hot.) A useful way to avoid confusing it with 「うちで」 is: 「うちで」defines a range for comparing things, whereas 「うちに」marks a time window in which to seize an opportunity to act.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q9.why.0: ✓ (a) The pattern 「〜うちに」combined with the dictionary-form verb 「いる」expresses taking the opportunity to go to Hokkaido while still living in Japan.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q9.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜うちで」is generally used to limit the scope of comparison within a group, not to express the period during which an action takes place.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q9.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜だけ」 means “only” and expresses limitation, so it is completely unsuitable for the meaning and context of wanting to carry out the action in this sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t22-q9.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜だけで」means “just with” or “only,” so using it in the sentence creates an incorrect grammar structure and makes the sentence meaningless.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) わりに
The grammar pattern 「〜わりに（は）」 expresses that the situation in the following clause is contrary to or disproportionate to what would be expected from the preceding clause.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q1.explanation: The grammar pattern「V（普）/ Aい / Aな / Nの ＋ わりに（は）」expresses that the result in the following clause does not match the level or standard normally expected from the preceding clause, often with a sense of surprise. In this sentence, it means: “Despite being so intelligent, that person cannot do the job very well.” Another typical example is:「このレストランは値段が安かったわりに、とても美味しかった。」(Although this restaurant was inexpensive, the food was surprisingly delicious.) Do not confuse it with「〜かわりに」, which expresses compensation, exchange, or substitution.「〜わりに」compares something with an implicit standard and highlights the mismatch.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜かわりに」 means substitution or compensation in exchange for something, and is not used to express a difference from the usual standard.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q1.why.1: ✓ (b) 「〜わりに（は）」 indicates that the situation in the following clause does not match the evaluation or degree expressed in the preceding clause (although someone is intelligent, they are actually unable to get things done).
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜とおりに」means “exactly as...” or “following...,” so it is completely unsuitable for connecting two contrasting clauses.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜うえに」means “not only... but also...” and adds information in the same direction. It does not express contrast.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q10.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 使わせていただき
This sentence requires a polite expression asking permission for the speaker to perform an action, using the causative construction together with the humble expression「〜（さ）せていただきませんか」.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q10.explanation: The pattern 「V-(さ)せていただきませんか」, consisting of a causative て-form followed by 「いただきませんか」, is polite and humble. It is used in formal communication when the speaker asks for permission to do something. The complete sentence means: “Excuse me, could you let me use your phone for a moment?” The key to avoiding confusion is identifying the subject of the action: because the speaker wants to use the phone, the verb must be changed to the causative form 「使わせて」(let me use it). This immediately rules out passive forms such as 「使われて」 in options (a) and (d). Another example is: 「風邪をひいたので、早退させていただきませんか。」(I have caught a cold, so may I leave early?)
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q10.why.0: ✗ (a) The passive form (使われて) is incorrect, and the conjugated form 「いただけ」 cannot be followed directly by 「〜ませんか」.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q10.why.1: ✓ (b) This correctly uses the polite permission-request structure 「V-させて＋いただきませんか」 (“Would you allow me to...?”), asking the other person for permission to use the phone.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q10.why.2: ✗ (c) This choice uses the wrong conjugated form of「いただく」when it is combined directly with the ending「〜ませんか」in the basic permission-request pattern.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q10.why.3: ✗ (d) The passive form 「使われて」is incorrect because the speaker is the person using the phone, not someone affected by the action.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q11.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) までに
The expression 「〜までに」 indicates a deadline by which a punctual action—in this case, submitting the report 「出してください」—must be completed, either before or no later than that time.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q11.explanation: The grammar pattern「Noun referring to a time / V-る ＋ までに」indicates a deadline: an action must be completed before or no later than the specified time. The complete sentence means: “As for the report, please be sure to submit it by 5:00 p.m. today.” To distinguish it from「まで」, remember that「まで」is used with verbs describing continuous actions, such as「待つ」and「働く」, whereas「までに」is used with one-time, completed actions, such as「出す」and「提出する」. Compare:「金曜日までに書類を準備してください」(Please prepare the documents by Friday).
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q11.why.0: ✗ (a) 「だけ」 expresses a limitation in scope (“only”); it is not used to indicate a deadline for completing an action.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q11.why.1: ✗ (b) 「まで」is used for an action or state that continues up to a time limit; it does not combine with a punctual action such as「出してください」.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q11.why.2: ✗ (c) 「だけに」means “precisely because..., all the more...,” so it is completely unsuitable in a context involving a submission deadline.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q11.why.3: ✓ (d) 「までに」indicates a final deadline, requiring the report to be submitted by 5:00 at the latest.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q12.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 子ども
The particle 「でさえ」 means “even” or “not even” and introduces an example at the minimum or simplest level. Therefore, “children” is the most suitable choice for emphasizing that the speaker could not solve an extremely easy question.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q12.explanation: The pattern「Noun + (で)さえ」means “even” or “not even” and is often used to give an extreme example at the minimum or simplest level, implying that more ordinary cases are naturally included. The complete sentence can be understood as: "Even a child could solve the puzzle, yet I could not answer it." Another example with the same pattern is:「仕事が忙しすぎて、昼ご飯を食べる時間さえありません」(I am so busy with work that I do not even have time to eat lunch). The key clue is the negative and regretful meaning in the following clause,「答えられなかった」, so the noun before「でさえ」must be「子ども」, the subject with the most basic ability, not「大人」or「先生」.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q12.why.0: ✗ (a) 大人(“adult”) refers to someone with full awareness, so being able to do the action is obvious and does not provide the extreme minimum example needed to combine with 「でさえ」in this context.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q12.why.1: ✓ (b) 子ども (children) represents the simplest level of understanding and combines perfectly with 「でさえ」 to emphasize how unusual it is that the speaker cannot solve such an easy question.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q12.why.2: ✗ (c) Since 先生 (teacher) is a highly knowledgeable professional, being able to answer is expected; it is not a suitable example of a beginner-level degree.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q12.why.3: ✗ (d) 男女 (men and women) is a noun referring to gender, not a level of understanding or degree of difficulty, so the resulting phrase is meaningless.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q13.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) なる
The purpose pattern「〜ために」requires a verb in the dictionary form (V-る) expressing a volitional action by the subject.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q13.explanation: The structure 「V-る / Nの + ために」 expresses purpose ("in order to / for..."), and the preceding action must be intentional and under the speaker's control; the two clauses also usually have the same subject. In the question, the complete sentence 「医者になるために、医学部に入った。」 means: "I entered medical school to become a doctor." Compare: 「家を買うために、毎月お金を貯金しています。」 (I save money every month to buy a house.) Learners often mistakenly choose (a) なれる, so remember the key point: intentional verbs are used with 「ために」, while potential or non-volitional verbs require 「ように」, as in 医者になれるように.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q13.why.0: ✗ (a) なれる is a potential-form verb belonging to the non-volitional group, so it cannot combine with ために; ように must be used to express purpose.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q13.why.1: ✓ (b) なる is a dictionary-form verb with volitional meaning, and it correctly combines with ために to express a clear purpose.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q13.why.2: ✗ (c) なった is a verb in the past form (V-た), so it does not follow the conjugation rule for the purpose pattern ために.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q13.why.3: ✗ (d) なりたい expresses a desire or wish and cannot be directly combined with ために to form an adverbial purpose clause.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q14.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) たびに
The structure V-る + たびに means “every time,” accurately describing Tanaka’s repeated habit whenever he visits this restaurant.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q14.explanation: The structure 「V-る / Nの ＋ たびに」 means “every time...” and describes an action or event that repeatedly occurs whenever the preceding condition appears, like a habit or regular pattern. The complete sentence means: “Every time Tanaka comes to this restaurant, he always orders ramen.” Compare: この曲を聞くたびに、学生時代の楽しかった思い出がよみがえる。(Every time I hear this song, happy memories of my student days come back to me.) A quick test-taking tip is to notice 「～ばかり」(always, nothing but...) in the second clause, indicating repeated behavior. This points to 「たびに」 and rules out 「うちに」(while there is an opportunity), 「までに」(by a deadline), and 「わりに」(compared with what is usual).
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q14.why.0: ✓ (a) The structure V-る + たびに means “every time…,” correctly expressing the subject's habit of ordering ramen whenever they visit this restaurant.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q14.why.1: ✗ (b) The structure うちに means “while” or “before the situation changes,” suggesting that something should be done while an opportunity lasts. It does not fit this sentence’s context.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q14.why.2: ✗ (c) The structure までに means “by/before,” indicating a deadline by which an action must be completed; it does not express a repeated action.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q14.why.3: ✗ (d) わりに means “relatively... compared with...” and indicates something contrary to expectations or the usual degree, so it does not have a suitable meaning here.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q15.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 落ちました
The particle「が」before the blank requires an intransitive verb describing an event that occurs on its own. Therefore, the past form of「落ちる」(to fall) is the only correct choice.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q15.explanation: The key point is distinguishing the familiar N3 pair of intransitive and transitive verbs. The intransitive verb 「落ちる」 (to fall) takes 「が」 in the pattern 「[object] が 落ちる」 to describe an event that occurs on its own, while the transitive verb 「落とす」 (to drop) takes 「を」 when an agent causes the object to fall. Since the key has just fallen onto the floor, speaker A uses the past form 「落ちました」 with the sentence-ending particle 「よ」 to promptly inform the other person. The complete exchange means: A: “Oh, you dropped your key!” B: “I wasn’t paying attention. Thank you!”. Compare: 「机の上からペンが落ちました。」 (A pen fell from the desk.) A quick test-taking tip: 「が」 goes with 「落ちる」, while 「を」 goes with 「落とす」.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q15.why.0: ✗ (a) 「落とす」is a transitive verb meaning “to drop” and requires its object to be marked with 「を」; it does not combine directly with 「が」in this context.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q15.why.1: ✗ (b) 「落とされました」 is the passive form of a transitive verb, so it is unnatural and inappropriate when reporting an object falling normally.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q15.why.2: ✓ (c) 「落ちる」is an intransitive verb used with the particle 「が」(かぎが落ちる) to report that the key has fallen.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q15.why.3: ✗ (d) 「落ちられました」is the passive form of an intransitive verb, with a troublesome or honorific nuance, and is grammatically incorrect in this sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 際
The pattern「〜の際（に）」means “when” or “on the occasion of” and is used in formal instructions to indicate when an action should be performed.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q2.explanation: The structure 「N の際（に）」 or 「V-る / V-た 際（に）」 means “when” or “on the occasion of,” with a more formal and polite tone than 「〜とき」. It is commonly used in announcements, service instructions, and business communication. In the test sentence, 「ご注文の際には、ベルを押してください」 means: “When placing your order, please press the bell.” A similar example is: 「非常の際は、非常口から避難してください」(In an emergency, please evacuate through the emergency exit.) To distinguish it from 「うち」, note that 「うちに」 emphasizes taking the opportunity to do something before a situation changes, while 「際に」 simply identifies the formal occasion or time of an event.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q2.why.0: ✓ (a) 「〜の際（に）」means “when” or “on the occasion of,” and combines with the noun「ご注文」to indicate the time of ordering politely.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) 「まで」means “until,” so it is semantically unsuitable for indicating when to ring the bell.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) 「うち」 describes taking the opportunity to do something while a state is ongoing; it is not used for instructions tied to a specific event or point in time.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) 「ほど」indicates degree, approximate amount, or comparison, and has no function indicating a point in time.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 食べた
The pattern 「Vた + ばかりだ」expresses that an action has just finished, according to the speaker's subjective sense of elapsed time.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q3.explanation: The N3 grammar pattern「Vた + ばかりだ」uses the past short form (た-form) to express that something has just happened or was completed recently, based on the speaker’s subjective perception. In the sentence「夕飯はさっき食べたばかりだ。」, the meaning is: “I just finished eating dinner a little while ago.” Another typical example is: 「先月、日本に来たばかりなので、まだ生活に慣れていません。」(I only came to Japan last month, so I am not used to life here yet.) In the exam, look for time expressions indicating that only a short time has passed, such as「さっき」(a little while ago), and do not confuse it with「Vているばかり」, which has the negative meaning of “doing nothing but V” or “spending all one’s time V-ing.”
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) The pattern describing something that has just been completed does not combine a Vて-form verb with ばかりだ.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because 「Vる + ばかりだ」indicates an unfavorable trend that is continuing or something that is about to be done, and cannot be combined with the past-time adverb 「さっき」.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q3.why.2: ✓ (c) The past form 「Vた」combines with 「ばかりだ」to form the grammar pattern meaning that an action has just been completed.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q3.why.3: ✗ (d) The progressive form「Vている + ばかりだ」has a complaining nuance of “doing nothing but... all day”; it does not express something that has just happened.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) しか
Following the dictionary-form verb (買う), the pattern「〜しかなかった」expresses that there was no choice but to carry out that action.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q4.explanation: The grammar pattern 「V-る + しかない」(past: 「〜しかなかった」) means “there is no choice but to...” or “can only...,” expressing reluctance when no other option remains. In the exercise sentence, it means: “Because I did not have enough money, I had no choice but to buy the cheaper one.” Unlike 「だけ」, which mainly limits the scope in affirmative sentences, 「しか」must be followed by a negative ending such as 「ない／なかった」. Contrastive example: 「終電に乗り遅れたので、歩いて帰るしかなかった。」(I missed the last train, so I had no choice but to walk home.)
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q4.why.0: ✗ (a) 「さえ」means “even” or “to the extent that,” and cannot combine with a dictionary-form verb and the negative ending「なかった」to create an appropriate sentence pattern.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) 「まで」indicates a limit of range or degree, and it does not occur in the pattern 「V-る + までなかった」in this context.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) 「だけ」means “only,” but Japanese does not use the combination 「V-る + だけなかった」to express having no choice or reluctantly doing something.
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q4.why.3: ✓ (d) 「しか」 follows a verb in the dictionary form and combines with a negative predicate to form 「V-る + しかない／しかなかった」, meaning “there is no choice but to” or “one must.”
default.q.15day_n3-t23-q5.verdict:

Learners may be tempted to use the past form「帰った」because returning is a completed action, but「以来」must be attached to the conjunctive「て」form to link the starting event with the continuing state.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q4.why.0: ✗ (a) 帰る is the dictionary form and cannot be combined with 「以来」according to the grammar rules.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) 帰った is the past form and is not the form required by the pattern 「～て以来」.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q4.why.2: ✓ (c) 帰って is the te-form of the verb and correctly forms the pattern「V-て以来」.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) 帰り is the stem formed by removing ます, so it cannot appropriately precede the particle 「以来」.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q5.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) は
The particle 「は」 combines with the negative predicate 「いない」 to complete the superlative comparison pattern 「N1 ほど… N2 はいない」, implying that nobody surpasses N1.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q5.explanation: The pattern 「N1 ほど ＋ (modifying clause) ＋ N2 ＋ はない／はいない」expresses the speaker's subjective judgment that no other person or thing reaches N1's level; in other words, N1 is the best within that scope. In this sentence, the particle 「は」after 「教え方がおもしろい先生」highlights the subject before the negative predicate 「いない」. The complete meaning is: "There is no teacher whose way of teaching is as engaging as that teacher's." Compare it with: 「健康ほど大切なものはない。」(Nothing is more important than health.) When 「…ほど」appears in the first clause and the sentence ends in 「ない／いない」, choose 「は」according to this standard pattern rather than degree adverbs such as 「さえ」or emphatic particles such as 「こそ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q5.why.0: ✗ (a) The particle 「に」 generally indicates a place, time, or recipient of an action. It is not suitable for linking a noun to the negative predicate 「いない」 in this comparison.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q5.why.1: ✗ (b) 「こそ」 emphasizes or asserts “precisely,” and does not combine with the negative predicate 「いない」 to form a superlative comparison.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q5.why.2: ✗ (c) 「さえ」means “even” or “as much as,” and does not form a complete superlative comparison when combined with 「ほど」.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q5.why.3: ✓ (d) 「は」marks the noun phrase as the topic being negated, fitting the standard pattern「N1 ほど… N2 はいない」perfectly.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q6.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) にしては
The grammar pattern 「〜にしては」is used to express that the road being crowded is contrary to what would normally be expected during the daytime.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q6.explanation: The structure 「N / plain form (Na-adjective or noun without だ) + にしては」 means “although...,” and is used when the actual situation or degree differs from the usual standard or expectation, often with a sense of surprise. In the test context, the complete sentence means: “Although it was the middle of the day, the streets were surprisingly crowded.” Compare: 「この時計は安かったにしては、何年も壊れずに動いている。」 (“Although this watch was cheap, it has been running for years without breaking.”) Do not confuse it with 「〜の反面」, which compares two contrasting aspects that coexist in the same subject, such as advantages and disadvantages. 「〜にしては」 contrasts an unexpected reality with a specific standard.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q6.why.0: ✓ (a) It follows the noun 「昼間」 directly to describe the actual situation being crowded, contrary to the usual expectation for daytime.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q6.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜の反面」describes two contrasting aspects of the same thing or situation; it is not used for something contrary to expectations.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q6.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜ほど」 is used for comparison or degree and combines directly with a noun; it does not go with 「なほど」.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q6.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜だからって」means "just because..." and is usually followed by a negative form; it is not used to describe a current state.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q7.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 見せてもらった
With 「に」marking the person who performs the action, 「V-てもらう」expresses receiving someone’s help—in this case, being allowed to look at a book (見せる).
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q7.explanation: The grammar pattern「[person performing the action] に + V-てもらう」describes the speaker receiving a beneficial action from someone else. Here, the seatmate performs the action "show," 見せる, so it changes to「見せてもらった」. The complete sentence translates as: 'Because I had left my textbook at home, my seatmate let me look at theirs.' Example: 友達に旅行の写真を見せてもらいました (My friend showed me their travel photos). A useful test-taking tip is to focus on the particle: the presence of「隣の人に」rules out「～てくれた」, which normally requires the performer to be marked by が or は. Then distinguish 見る (look at) from 見せる (show someone).
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q7.why.0: ✗ (a) 「見てもらう」means “to have someone look at or check something for you,” such as having a teacher check your work; it does not fit the situation of wanting to look at a friend’s book.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q7.why.1: ✓ (b) 「見せてもらう」combines the transitive verb 見せる (“show”) with the benefactive expression てもらう, correctly expressing that the speaker is allowed to look at the book by the person sitting nearby.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q7.why.2: ✗ (c) 「見てくれた」 is incorrect in meaning—it means “looked at it for someone” rather than “let someone see it”—and is also grammatically wrong because the person performing the action should be marked by に, not が/は.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q7.why.3: ✗ (d) 「見せてくれた」is correct only when the person showing something is the subject marked by が/は, as in「隣の人が...」; it does not follow「隣の人に」as in the question.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q8.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 聞こうとしない
The grammar pattern 「〜ようとしない」describes a third-person subject who has no intention of performing an action or stubbornly refuses to do it.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q8.explanation: The pattern 「V-よう＋としない」(the volitional form + としない) describes another person's stubborn refusal or firm unwillingness to do something despite being urged or advised. The complete sentence means: "No matter how sternly I warn her, she still refuses to listen." Compare it with: 「息子はいくら注意しても、野菜を食べようとしない。」(No matter how many times I warn my son, he still refuses to eat vegetables.) A quick recognition tip is that when concessive expressions such as 「どんなに／いくら〜ても」occur with another person who is being uncooperative, think of the negative volitional pattern「〜ようとしない」rather than affirmative patterns or expressions of situational solutions.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q8.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜こともない」 means “there is no need to...” or “it has never happened,” and does not express a stubborn refusal to listen.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q8.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜しかない」means “there is no choice but to” or “have to,” which is the complete opposite of a context denying the act of complying.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q8.why.2: ✓ (c) 「〜ようとしない」combines with the volitional form of a verb to indicate that the other person firmly refuses to listen, which fits the concessive clause “no matter how strongly one speaks.”
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q8.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜ないことはない」 means “it is not that I do not listen,” expressing hesitant affirmation and completely distorting the logic of the sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q9.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) お目にかかって
Because the speaker is the one meeting the other person, the special humble form of 「会う」, 「お目にかかる」, must be used.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q9.explanation: In formal communication, 「お目にかかる」 is the special humble form (謙譲語 I) of 「会う」. It follows the structure 「[superior person/business partner] に + お目にかかる」, lowering the speaker and showing respect toward the person being met. The sentence means: "Earlier, I had the opportunity to meet Mr. Tanaka and greet him." A similar example is: 「明日、支社長に初めてお目にかかる予定です。」(I am scheduled to meet the branch manager for the first time tomorrow.) An important distinction is between 「お目にかかる」 and 「拝見する」. Although both involve the eyes, 「拝見する」 is used for viewing documents or letters, while meeting a person requires 「お目にかかる」.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q9.why.0: ✗ (a) 「ご覧になる」is the respectful form of 「見る」(to look at, watch), used to honor another person’s action, not one’s own.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q9.why.1: ✗ (b) 「拝見する」is the humble form of「見る」and is used when the speaker looks at or reads an object or document, not when looking at a person.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q9.why.2: ✓ (c) 「お目にかかる」is the humble form of「会う」and is correctly used to describe the speaker meeting a superior or business partner.
default.q.15day_n3-t24-q9.why.3: ✗ (d) 「うかがう」 is the humble form of 「聞く・訪ねる」 (to ask, listen, or visit), and does not mean to meet someone.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) ほど
The structure 「V-る + ほど」indicates the degree of the action in the following clause, showing that the drinking reached the point of causing physical discomfort and nausea.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q1.explanation: The pattern 「V (dictionary/plain form) + ほど」 expresses that the degree of an action or state in the following clause is as great as described in the preceding clause. In this sentence, the complete meaning is: "Last night, I accidentally drank so much that I felt sick and uncomfortable." To express "to the extent that," Japanese uses 「ほど」 (or 「くらい」), not 「ように」 (which expresses a purpose, "so that") or 「ばかり」 (which means "only/all" or "just"). Another example:「足が棒になるほど歩いた。」(I walked so much that my legs felt like sticks.)
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) 「ほど」combines with a verb in the dictionary form to express 'to the extent that,' clarifying that the drinking was excessive enough to cause discomfort.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) 「よう」is commonly used to express purpose (〜ように) or similarity; the form「なるよう」is not used to indicate the degree of a result that has already occurred.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) 「ばかり」means “nothing but” or “have just done something”; it cannot follow a dictionary-form verb to express the degree “to the extent that.”
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) 「こそ」 is an emphasis particle meaning “precisely” or “it is precisely because...,” so it is completely inappropriate grammatically and semantically for expressing degree.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q10.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 欲しがって
The blank comes before the auxiliary verb いる to describe a third person’s continuing desire (弟), so the adjective 欲しい must become the verb 欲しがる and be conjugated into the te-form.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q10.explanation: In Japanese, a third person’s desire is not directly expressed with 欲しい. Instead, 欲しい changes to the verb 欲しがる (remove い and add がる), which describes the desire as outwardly observable, and it takes the particle を. When the desire continues as a psychological state, especially with the adverb ずっと, it combines with the auxiliary verb いる to form 欲しがっている. The complete sentence translates as: “Recently, my younger brother has been constantly wishing for a new computer.” A similar example is:「あの子はずっと新しいおもちゃを欲しがっている。」(That child has been demanding a new toy for a long time.) Be careful not to confuse this with 欲しそうに or 欲しそうで: the suffix そう expresses an inference based on outward appearance, as in 欲しそうに見ている (looking at it as if they want it), whereas 欲しがる expresses the other person’s clearly observable desire and combines with いる.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q10.why.0: ✗ (a) The past form 欲しがった cannot be directly combined with the auxiliary verb いる afterward.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q10.why.1: ✓ (b) The verb 欲しがる changes to the te-form 欲しがって, which combines perfectly with いる to form the progressive construction.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q10.why.2: ✗ (c) 欲しそうで is the te-form of the conjectural form そうだ, so it cannot be combined with the auxiliary verb いる in this pattern.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q10.why.3: ✗ (d) 欲しそうに is an adverb that modifies an action verb; it does not directly combine with いる as the predicate.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q11.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) に比べて
The sentence uses the past reference point 「以前」as a standard for comparison with present progress, so the comparison pattern 「に比べて」is the only correct choice.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q11.explanation: The structure 「N / [V-plain form + の] + に比べて」 means “compared with...” and is used when a noun or point in time serves as the standard of comparison, highlighting a difference in quality or degree in the following clause. The complete sentence means: “Compared with before, Ms. Hara has gradually been making far fewer mistakes.” For a deeper understanding, consider: 「今年の夏は去年に比べてとても涼しい。」(This summer is much cooler than last summer.) To avoid confusion, note that 「に対して」 usually indicates a contrast between two opposing sides or objects, while 「に比べて」 focuses on the difference in degree and often appears with expressions of change such as 「だいぶ」(considerably) or 「〜ようになってきた」(has gradually come to...).
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q11.why.0: ✗ (a) The pattern 「〜によって」 indicates a cause, method, or variation depending on the object; it is not used to establish a comparison standard.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q11.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern「〜に対して」indicates a target or a contrast between two things; it is not used to measure the degree of change over time.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q11.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜になって」 expresses a change of state or the arrival of a new point in time; it does not fit appropriately with the following clause in this context.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q11.why.3: ✓ (d) The pattern「〜に比べて」combines with the time-related noun「以前」(以前, “before”) as the basis of comparison, highlighting the positive change in the following clause.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q12.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) ついでに
The grammar pattern 「～ついでに」 means “while you are at it” or “incidentally,” and is used when taking advantage of an existing action or trip to do something else as well.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q12.explanation: The grammar pattern「V-る / V-た / N-の + ついでに」means “while you are at it” or “incidentally.” It is used when someone takes advantage of an existing main action to do an additional, secondary task. In the test context, going to the convenience store is the main action, while withdrawing money from the ATM is the additional action. The complete translation is: “While stopping by the convenience store, I withdrew 30,000 yen from the ATM.” Compare:「散歩のついでに、ポストに手紙を出してきました。」(While I was out for a walk, I also mailed a letter). To avoid choosing (d), remember that「～につれて」always includes the particle「に」and describes proportional change (as A changes, B changes), not two independent actions combined with「ついでに」.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q12.why.0: ✗ (a) 「～を通じて」 means “through” or “throughout,” and is completely inappropriate in the context of withdrawing money at a convenience store.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q12.why.1: ✓ (b) 「～ついでに」 follows the dictionary form of a verb, 「行く」, and means “while you are there” or “on the way.” It accurately expresses withdrawing money while stopping by a convenience store.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q12.why.2: ✗ (c) 「いっしょに」 means “together” and is commonly used in 「～と一緒に」 to indicate the person performing an action together with someone; it does not directly follow a verb in the dictionary form.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q12.why.3: ✗ (d) 「つれて」 is commonly used in the pattern 「～につれて」 to express a change in which two aspects develop together (the more..., the more...), and cannot directly follow a verb to connect incidental actions.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q13.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 一方で
The structure 「V-る + 一方で」combined with a verb expressing change indicates that something continues developing in one direction, becoming increasingly negative.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q13.explanation: The grammar pattern 「V-る + 一方で」 can combine with verbs describing change, such as 増える, 悪化する, and ひどくなる, to express a continuing trend that does not stop, often with a negative or worrying implication. The complete translation is: “I have had a cold since last week, but it just keeps getting worse instead of improving at all.” Another example is 「最近は仕事が忙しくなる一方で、休む暇もありません。」 (“Recently, work keeps getting busier, and I do not even have time to rest.”) Distinguish it from 「〜にしたがって」: the latter requires the following clause to describe a corresponding change, whereas 「一方だ／一方で」 emphasizes a one-directional, accelerating trend.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q13.why.0: ✗ (a) The pattern 「〜かわりに」means replacement or compensation for an action, so it is not appropriate for expressing the progression of an illness.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q13.why.1: ✗ (b) The suffix 「〜気味」follows a noun or the ます-stem of a verb, so it cannot be attached directly to the dictionary form 「ひどくなる」.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q13.why.2: ✓ (c) The structure 「V-る + 一方で」combines with a verb expressing change to describe a negative situation becoming increasingly serious.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q13.why.3: ✗ (d) The grammar「〜にしたがって」requires the following clause to describe a parallel change; it cannot be followed by the static negative result「全然よくなりません」.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q14.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) さえ
The particle さえ means “even” or “to the extent that.” Combined with the following negative clause, it emphasizes being so busy that even the basic act of eating lunch could not be done.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q14.explanation: The grammar pattern「N + さえ」means “even,” “including,” or “as much as,” and highlights something obvious or minimal. It implies that if even this basic thing cannot be done, other things are even less possible, so the following clause very often uses the negative form. The complete sentence means: "I was so busy with work today that I did not even have a little time for lunch." Another typical example is: 「足の痛みがひどくて、歩くことさえできません。」(My legs hurt so badly that I cannot even walk.) Note the distinction:「くらい / ほど」expresses a general degree (“to the extent that”), whereas「さえ」attaches directly to an extreme noun or item to emphasize the speaker’s difficult circumstances.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q14.why.0: ✗ (a) ほど generally indicates an equivalent degree or an approximate amount. It does not carry the emphasis of a minimum example in a negative sentence, as さえ does.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q14.why.1: ✓ (b) さえmeans “even” or “as much as,” presenting an extreme or minimal case to emphasize the seriousness of the situation when used with the negative 「ありませんでした」.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q14.why.2: ✗ (c) くらい mainly indicates an approximate degree or a relatively mild extent; it does not express an extreme degree or strongly emphasize a clear lack as さえ does.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q14.why.3: ✗ (d) には is generally used to indicate a purpose or limit the recipient or target, so it does not create a logical semantic connection in this sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q15.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 最中に
The pattern 「N の最中に」describes an unexpected or unwanted event occurring precisely while an action or event is at its height.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q15.explanation: The pattern 「V-ている / N の + 最中（に）」emphasizes that something occurs right in the middle of an intense or ongoing activity. The following clause often describes a sudden disruptive incident. The complete sentence means: "Yesterday, I got a stomachache right in the middle of taking an exam." Example: 「会議の最中に、突然停電してしまった。」(The power suddenly went out in the middle of the meeting.) Do not confuse it with 「〜うちに」: 「最中に」is commonly associated with an unexpected, troublesome interruption, whereas 「うちに」often expresses the intention to do something before conditions change.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q15.why.0: ✓ (a) The structure 「N の最中に」is correctly combined with the noun 試験 to express having a sudden stomachache while taking an exam.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q15.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「〜うちに」describes taking action before a state changes or a natural transformation occurs; it is not used for an unexpected event that interrupts something.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q15.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜にかけて」indicates an approximate span of time or space from one point to another; it is not used to locate the specific time when an incident occurred.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q15.why.3: ✗ (d) The expression「〜のわけで」is not a structure indicating a point in time and is grammatically and semantically incorrect in this context.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) としても
The structure 「たとえ〜としても」expresses a concessive hypothetical meaning “even if” or “even though,” emphasizing that even if the situation in the preceding clause does not succeed, the previous effort is not wasted.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q2.explanation: The pattern 「たとえ ＋ [plain form] ＋ としても」, used with verbs, i-adjectives, na-adjectives, or nouns, introduces a concessive assumption ("even if..."), emphasizing that even if the negative situation in the first clause occurs, it will not change the result or fact in the second clause. The exercise sentence can be translated in full as: "Even if you do not succeed this time, all the effort you have made up to now will not have been wasted." As a similar example, consider: 「たとえ失敗したとしても、最後まで諦めずに挑戦し続ける。」 (Even if I fail, I will continue trying without giving up until the end.) For test-taking purposes, when you see the adverb 「たとえ」 at the beginning of a sentence, immediately think of the familiar concessive pair 「たとえ〜ても / たとえ〜としても」 and eliminate the easily confused pattern 「〜とすると」, which expresses a logical supposition meaning "assuming that...".
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q2.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜にとって」 indicates a standpoint or evaluative perspective (“for…”), and does not combine with the hypothetical adverb 「たとえ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜にとっても」 means “even for...” and adds emphasis to another subject; it does not combine with the plain form of a verb to create a concessive hypothetical clause.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q2.why.2: ✓ (c) 「〜としても」combines perfectly with the adverb 「たとえ」to form the grammar pattern 「たとえ〜としても」, meaning “even if...” or “even supposing that...,” and it fits both the structure and meaning.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜とすると」expresses a simple hypothetical assumption, “if that is the case,” and is not used to express concession or combine with 「たとえ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) わけがない
Based on Yamamoto’s serious personality, the speaker confidently asserts that lying is absolutely impossible for him.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q3.explanation: The pattern 「plain-form V + わけがない」, equivalent to 「はずがない」, firmly states that something is absolutely impossible, based on evidence or logical reasoning. Given the emphasis on the person’s character in the first clause, the complete sentence means: "There’s no way someone as upright and serious as Mr. Yamamoto would lie!" Compare: 「これだけしっかり準備したのだから、失敗するわけがない。」 (We prepared this thoroughly, so there’s no way we’ll fail.) To distinguish N3 patterns containing 「わけ」, remember: 「〜わけがない」 denies all possibility (absolutely impossible); 「〜わけではない」 denies only part of a statement (not necessarily/not exactly); and 「〜わけにはいかない」 means that one cannot do something because of responsibility, morality, or social rules.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) 「わけだ」is used to explain an inevitable reason or obvious conclusion (“no wonder,” “that explains why”), not to deny the possibility of an action occurring.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q3.why.1: ✓ (b) 「わけがない」expresses strong negation (“there is no way” or “it is absolutely impossible”), which fits the premise that Mr. Yamamoto is very serious.
default.q.15day_n3-t25-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) 「わけではない」 expresses partial negation (“not necessarily,” “it is not that...”), so it cannot convey absolute trust in the other person.

The key point is that 「〜が流れていた」(was being broadcast) naturally combines with an audio announcement 「アナウンス」, not with 「アドバイス」(advice), which combines with verbs such as 「もらう」or「する」.

The verb phrase 「世話をする」 describes caring for, watering, or nurturing living things. Combined with 「庭の草花」 (“the plants and flowers in the garden”), it forms the most natural and accurate expression.

default.q.15day_n3-t72-q17.why.2: ✗ (c) To express chatting with friends over the phone, verbs such as 話す or おしゃべりする must be used instead of 世話をする.
default.q.15day_n3-t72-q17.why.3: ✗ (d) If someone makes a serious mistake and is reprimanded or scolded by a superior, the passive form of a reprimanding verb, such as 叱られた or 怒られた, is required. 世話をする does not mean to discipline someone.

default.q.15day_n3-t72-q18.why.1: ✗ (b) To express making plans or intending to travel with friends, use 「計画」(plan) or 「予定」(予定).

The complete sentence means: "It is pleasantly sunny today, so it is fairly warm outside." Compare it with: 「深夜に大声で騒ぐのは非常識な行為です。」(Making a lot of noise late at night is an inconsiderate act.) To distinguish the negative prefixes at the N3 level, remember: 「不」negates an ordinary quality (inconvenient, uneasy), 「無」means something is completely absent (irresponsible, meaningless), 「未」means something has not yet occurred (minor, undecided), and 「非」refers to something that deviates from common rules or standards (unreasonable, unofficial).

default.q.15day_n3-t75-q10.why.3: ✗ (d) The prefix 「未」means that an action or state is incomplete, as in 未完成 and 未成年; it does not combine with 「常識」.

default.q.15day_n3-t75-q12.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 興奮
Thinking about tomorrow’s performance makes the speaker so excited and stimulated that they cannot sleep. Therefore, the word expressing intense excitement, 興奮 (こうふん), is the most appropriate choice.
default.q.15day_n3-t75-q12.explanation: The key vocabulary item is the noun「興奮」(こうふん), which commonly combines with「する」to form the Group 3 verb「興奮する」. It describes an intense emotional state of excitement, exhilaration, or agitation before a highly anticipated event or an unexpected occurrence. The complete sentence means: "Just thinking about tomorrow's concert makes me so excited that I cannot get a wink of sleep." Another example is: 試合で劇的な逆転勝利を収め、サポーターたちは興奮して叫び続けた。(The team achieved a dramatic comeback victory, and the supporters continued shouting excitedly.) A useful test-taking tip is to notice the physiological consequence「眠れない」(cannot sleep) in the following clause; among the four choices, only「興奮」has the strong mental-stimulation nuance that can lead to insomnia, unlike「想像」(merely thinking or imagining something) or「満足」(a feeling of satisfaction that comes only after an experience is complete).
default.q.15day_n3-t75-q12.why.0: ✗ (a) 感心 means admiration or being impressed, and is used to praise or admire another person’s actions or good qualities, not to describe one’s own excitement.
default.q.15day_n3-t75-q12.why.1: ✗ (b) 想像 means mentally picturing something; it does not convey the overwhelming emotion that causes sleeplessness in this context.
default.q.15day_n3-t75-q12.why.2: ✓ (c) 興奮 means excitement or heightened emotional stimulation, accurately describing the intense anticipation of a major event that prevents someone from sleeping.
default.q.15day_n3-t75-q12.why.3: ✗ (d) 満足 (satisfaction, contentment) describes a feeling of fulfillment after achieving a desired result, so it cannot be used before the event actually takes place.
default.q.15day_n3-t75-q13.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) なるべく
The adverb 「なるべく」expresses making an effort to do something as much as possible within one's limits. It combines naturally with 「早く」to express trying to arrange to return home early tonight.
default.q.15day_n3-t75-q13.explanation: The adverb 「なるべく」 usually comes before degree adverbs or verbs expressing intention or desire. It describes making an effort to do something within the limits of what is possible, without implying an obligation. Thus, 「今夜はなるべく早く帰るつもりだ。」 means: "I plan to try to get home as early as possible tonight." A common conversational example is 「なるべく早くお返事をいただけますか。」 (Could you please reply as soon as possible?). default.q.15day_n3-t75-q13.why.1: ✗ (b) 「ついに」indicates an outcome or result achieved after a long period of anticipation; it is not used to modify a future intention such as 「〜つもりだ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t75-q13.why.2: ✗ (c) 「いきなり」refers to an action or event happening suddenly and unexpectedly, which completely conflicts with a preplanned action.
default.q.15day_n3-t75-q13.why.3: ✗ (d) 「たいてい」describes frequency or usual present habits, so it is not appropriate for a personal plan concerning a specific evening, 「今夜」.

In the JLPT, when you see adverbs expressing absolute completeness such as「全部」or「すべて」, favor「〜きる」over「〜すぎる」, which only means “too much.”

default.q.15day_n3-t75-q16.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) ぴったりだ
When discussing the size of clothing or shoes,「ぴったりだ」is directly synonymous with「ちょうどいい」, meaning a perfect fit.

To avoid confusing N3 reduplicated words ending in 「～り」, remember: 「ぴったり」 means a perfect fit, 「そっくり」 means identical, 「すっきり」 means refreshed or uncluttered, and 「しっかり」 means firm or reliable.

It expresses the subjective evaluation that N1 is the best or greatest, with no other object reaching the same level. default.q.15day_n3-t76-q20.why.1: ✗ (b) The particle 「こそ」 adds emphasis, meaning “precisely” or “indeed”; it does not combine with the negative predicate 「いない」 to form a comparison structure.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q20.why.2: ✗ (c) The particle 「さえ」means “even,” and does not fit a superlative comparison expressing the speaker’s assessment of the highest degree.

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q21.verdict:

Remember that 「にしては」 is based on a specific standard or fact and expresses surprise, unlike 「反面」, which presents two parallel aspects, or 「ほど」, which compares degree.

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q22.why.3: ✗ (d) The structure ～てくれる requires the person performing the action to be marked with が or は, not に.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q23.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 聞こうとしない

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q23.explanation: The key grammar pattern is 「Vよう＋としない」, in which a verb is put into the volitional form before 「としない」. It describes the speaker's frustration or helplessness when a third person stubbornly refuses to do something. In this context, the completed sentence means: "No matter how sternly I warn her, she stubbornly refuses to listen." This pattern often appears with adverbs expressing unsuccessful attempts to influence someone, such as 「どんなに…ても」 or 「いくら…ても」. The verb must be in the volitional form, as in 聞こう, emphasizing the other person's unwillingness. This is completely different from 「Vる＋こともない」("there is no need to do") and 「Vる＋しかない」("there is no choice but to do"). default.q.15day_n3-t76-q23.why.2: ✓ (c) The pattern 「Vよう＋としない」 describes a third-person subject stubbornly refusing to perform an action (“will not listen”), which perfectly matches the context 「どんなに強く言っても」.

Following the emphatic reason pattern 「〜からこそ」, the correct order is 2 - 1 - 3 - 4 (一生懸命勉強したからこそ合格できた), so the third starred position is 「こそ」.

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q25.why.1: ✗ (b) 「勉強した」occupies position 1 immediately after the adverb 「一生懸命」and serves as the predicate of the cause clause.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q25.why.2: ✓ (c) 「こそ」goes in the third position marked with an asterisk and follows 「から」to form the emphatic pattern 「〜からこそ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q25.why.3: ✗ (d) 「合格できた」expresses an achieved result, so it must come fourth as the sentence-final predicate.

It expresses an overwhelming emotion, desire, or feeling that arises naturally and cannot be controlled. In addition, the particle 「なんて」after the dictionary form verb 「負ける」emphasizes surprise, anger, or contempt toward an event. The complete sentence 「あんな男に負けるなんてくやしくて仕方がなかった」means: "Losing to a man like him made me so frustrated and angry that I could hardly stand it." For a quick solution, look at the end of the sentence: 「なかった」combined with 「仕方が」forms 「仕方がなかった」, so the only te-form among the four choices, 「くやしくて」, must come immediately before it in the third position.

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q26.why.3: ✗ (d) なんて follows the dictionary form「負ける」and expresses disapproval, so it goes in the second position.

✅ Correct answer: (d) きぼう

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q3.explanation: The word「希望」(きぼう) means hope, expectation, desire, or wish. It can be used independently as a noun or combined with the verb「希望する」. The sentence「食事について、何かご希望はありますか」means: "Do you have any requests or preferences regarding the meal?" Reference example:「お客様のご希望に合わせてプランを変更いたします」(We will adjust the plan to meet your preferences). default.q.15day_n3-t76-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) 「希」is pronounced「き」and does not undergo voicing to become「ぎ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) Incorrect because 望 does not have the half-voiced reading 「ぽう」 in this vocabulary item.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q3.why.3: ✓ (d) Correct because the standard on-reading of the Sino-Japanese word「希望」is「きぼう」.

✅ Correct answer: (c) うつくしい

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) 「やさしい」 corresponds to 「優しい」 (kind, gentle) or 「易しい」 (easy).
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q4.why.2: ✓ (c) The kanji 「美」 combined with the ending 「しい」 is correctly read as 「うつくしい」.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) 「したしい」is the reading of the kanji「親しい」, meaning close or familiar.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q5.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) おって

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q5.why.0: ✗ (a) うって is the te-form of 打つ, meaning to hit or type, not the reading of 折.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q5.why.1: ✗ (b) きって is the te-form of the verb 切る (to cut), with a completely different meaning and kanji from those in the question.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q5.why.2: ✗ (c) ふって is the te-form of 振る, meaning to wave or shake, and does not correspond to the kanji 折.
default.q.15day_n3-t76-q5.why.3: ✓ (d) おって is the て-form of 折る (to break or snap), which correctly matches the kanji 折 in the context of a broken bone.

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q8.verdict:

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q9.verdict:

default.q.15day_n3-t76-q9.why.1: ✓ (b) The verb 治る is correctly written with 治, and its correct past form is 治った.

default.q.15day_n3-t81-q10.explanation: In Japanese, the key word 「安心」 (あんしん) is both a noun and a noun that combines with 「する」 to form a verb. In the question, it appears in the potential form 「安心できます」 and conveys relief and peace of mind after anxiety or worry has been removed. The complete sentence 「家族といるときが、一番安心できます」 means: “I feel most at ease when I am with my family.” Another example is: 「彼の無事な顔を見て、とても安心しました」 (When I saw his unharmed face, I felt very relieved.) For JLPT purposes, distinguish 「心」 (“heart,” inner feelings) from 「信」, as in 信用 (trust) and 通信 (communication). Also distinguish 「安」 from 「案」, as in 案内 (guidance) and 提案 (proposal), which has the 木 component at the bottom.

default.q.15day_n3-t81-q10.why.2: ✓ (c) 安心 is the correct kanji spelling for a feeling of security and freedom from worry, making it fully appropriate in this sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t81-q10.why.3: ✗ (d) 信 (しん in 信頼, “trust”) has the on-reading 「しん」, but 安信 is an incorrect word and is not used to express peace of mind.

In the sentence 「毎日同じことばかりで、もう飽きてしまった。」, the meaning is: “Every day is just the same, so I am completely fed up with it.” Example: 「子供はどんなに高いおもちゃでも、すぐに飽きてしまう。」(Children quickly get tired of even the most expensive toys.) For the JLPT, distinguish the intended recipient: ask a teacher about knowledge with 「質問する」, ask relatives or strangers for everyday information with 「聞く／尋ねる」, and use 「問い合わせる」 for customer-to-organization inquiries.

Choice (a) means: “Because something urgent suddenly came up, next week’s trip had to be canceled.” For comparison: 「体調が悪いため、ホテルの予約をキャンセルしました。」(Because I was feeling unwell, I canceled my hotel reservation.) default.q.15day_n3-t81-q20.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) にともなって
This structure expresses one change occurring along with a corresponding change, which fits the sentence context.
default.q.15day_n3-t81-q20.explanation: The key grammar pattern is 「N / V-dictionary form・V-past form + の + に伴って」, meaning “along with / as A changes, B also changes.” It is commonly used in written or formal contexts to describe social phenomena or large-scale changes. The complete sentence can be translated as: “As the number of foreigners in the city increases, English signs have begun to appear everywhere.” A similar example is: 「時代の変化に伴って、人々の価値観も多様化してきた。」 (“Along with changes in the times, people’s values have gradually become more diverse.”) A useful test-taking clue is to look for words indicating change, such as 「増える」, 「減る」, and 「変化する」 in the first clause, combined with a change-of-state pattern such as 「〜ようになる」 in the second clause. This makes 「に伴って」 easy to identify and helps eliminate choices expressing an object or standpoint, such as 「に対して」 and 「にとって」.
default.q.15day_n3-t81-q20.why.0: ✓ (a) This accurately describes a parallel change: as the number of foreigners increases, English-language instructions also become more common.
default.q.15day_n3-t81-q20.why.1: ✗ (b) 「に対して」 means “toward/for” when expressing an attitude or action directed at an object, or “in contrast to.” It does not express a consequential change.
default.q.15day_n3-t81-q20.why.2: ✗ (c) 「にとって」means “for” or “from the standpoint of,” used to give an observation or evaluation from someone’s perspective; it does not fit the logic here.
default.q.15day_n3-t81-q20.why.3: ✗ (d) 「について」means “about” or “concerning,” indicating the topic of discussion or research, so its meaning is completely wrong in this context.

Also remember the key point: the two clauses connected by 「〜上に」must express evaluations in the same direction, not contrast. The complete sentence「山田さんが約束の時間に遅刻するなんて、何か理由があるに違いない」means: “For Mr. Yamada to be late for the appointed time, there must surely be some reason.” For this question, quickly identify the fixed ending「あるに」+「違いない」and the subject-predicate unit「何か理由がある」. This makes it easier to determine the order as b - a - d - c. Compare this example:「いつも元気な彼が学校を休むなんて、病気に違いない。」(For someone who is always energetic to miss school, he must be ill.)

default.q.15day_n3-t82-q26.why.1: ✗ (b) 「なんて」must appear immediately after the verb 「遅刻する」in the first position to express surprise; it cannot go in the starred position.
default.q.15day_n3-t82-q26.why.2: ✗ (c) 「あるに」must appear in the fourth position, immediately before 「違いない」, to form the conjectural structure 「あるに違いない」; it cannot go at the position marked by the asterisk.
default.q.15day_n3-t82-q26.why.3: ✓ (d) 「理由が」occupies position 3, the starred position, combining with 「何か」before it and serving as the subject of 「あるに」after it.

It attaches directly to a noun referring to the target group and has a formal tone, commonly appearing in public announcements or special offers. Here, 「学生の方に」 combines with 「限り」 to form 「学生の方に限り」. The price phrase 「５００円の」 modifies 「入場料」, producing: 「学生の方に限り、５００円の入場料が３００円になります」 (For students only, the 500-yen admission fee will be reduced to 300 yen). Another common example: 「本日に限り、全品2割引とさせていただきます」(For today only, all items will be 20% off.) When solving questions with 「限り」, first look for the noun followed by に and form the fixed phrase 「N に限り」.

default.q.15day_n3-t82-q27.why.3: ✗ (d) 学生の must come first as a modifier of the honorific noun 方; it does not belong in the starred position.

The complete sentence means: “If you hate your job that much, why don’t you try changing companies? default.q.15day_n3-t84-q42.explanation: The pattern 「noun + にわたって」, or にわたり / にわたる + noun, emphasizes that an action or phenomenon continues throughout a period, over a number of occasions, or across a wide geographical area. Exam tip: when you see a noun containing a clearly stated duration, such as three days or ten years, or a broad area such as the entire country or coastline, think of 「〜にわたって」 to emphasize scale. Do not confuse it with 「〜を通して」, which usually emphasizes continuity through a process or through a medium or intermediary.
default.q.15day_n3-t84-q42.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜に限って」 means “only” or “of all times, at precisely...,” and can also express a complaint; it does not fit a context describing the duration of time.
default.q.15day_n3-t84-q42.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜に対して」indicates the target of an action or contrast, so it cannot be used with a duration expression.
default.q.15day_n3-t84-q42.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜に関して」means “concerning” or “about” a topic and is used to introduce a subject for discussion, not to indicate the duration of an event.
default.q.15day_n3-t84-q42.why.3: ✓ (d) 「〜にわたって」 follows a noun indicating a period of time, such as ３日間, and expresses that an event continues throughout that period.

The structure 「V-る + には」 expresses a purpose and is followed by a necessary condition or requirement for achieving it.

The following clause usually states a necessary condition, obligation, or piece of advice, often with patterns such as「～なければならない」,「～が必要だ」, or「～べきだ」. In the question, the complete sentence means: "To become a doctor in the future, you must enter medical school." A similar example is「富士山に登るには、暖かい服を用意しておいたほうがいい。」(To climb Mount Fuji, you should prepare warm clothes in advance.) To avoid confusing it with「のに」, remember that when のに expresses purpose, it is commonly associated with the use of a tool or item, or with the amount of time or money required, whereas には emphasizes a prerequisite for achieving a goal.

default.q.15day_n3-t84-q48.why.3: ✗ (d) 「のに」expresses contrast (“although…,” “even though…”) or indicates the purpose for which something is used, often with an evaluation of time or cost; neither meaning fits this context.

default.q.15day_n3-t85-q34.explanation: The adverb 「今にも」 means “any moment now” and describes a change or action that appears about to happen, based on visual impressions. It almost always accompanies the conjectural pattern 「〜そうだ / 〜そうな」. The complete sentence (d) means: “That child looks as if they are about to burst into tears.” Another typical example is 「空が真っ暗になって、今にも雨が降り出しそうだ。」 (“The sky has become completely dark, and it looks as if it is about to start raining.”). default.q.15day_n3-t85-q35.explanation: The adverb「せっかく」has the nuance of having gone to considerable effort or finally receiving a valuable opportunity. It commonly combines with the plain form and「～のに／だが」to express regret or disappointment that one's effort was wasted. In the question, the complete sentence「せっかく料理を作ったのに、たくさん余ってしまった」means: "I went to all the trouble of cooking so many dishes, but in the end a lot was left over." Another contrasting example is:「せっかくの日曜日なのに、朝から雨でどこへも出かけられなかった。」("Even though it was a precious Sunday, it rained from the morning and I could not go anywhere.") default.q.15day_n3-t85-q35.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because when thanking someone for going out of their way and traveling a long distance to see you, Japanese uses the adverb 「わざわざ」.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q35.why.2: ✓ (c) Correct because 「せっかく～のに」fully expresses regret that, despite taking the trouble to cook, much of the food was left over.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q35.why.3: ✗ (d) When advising someone not to force themselves or go to unnecessary trouble under unfavorable circumstances, 「無理に」 or 「わざわざ」 should be used, not 「せっかく」.

default.q.15day_n3-t85-q36.why.3: ✗ (d) The structure 「Vた + きり」 expresses a state that has remained unchanged since an action was performed. It cannot be combined with 「～にしておく」 and is completely incorrect in meaning here.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q37.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) つけっぱなし
This pattern describes an action that was performed but whose resulting state was left unchanged without being dealt with further.

The complete sentence means: "I was so tired yesterday that I fell asleep with the TV left on." Compare: 「エアコンをつけっぱなしで出かけてしまった。」 (I accidentally left the air conditioner running when I went out.) Do not confuse it with (c) 「V-たて」. Although both follow the verb stem, 「～たて」 means "freshly made or done" and has a positive sense, as in 焼きたてのパン (freshly baked bread), whereas 「～っぱなし」 conveys neglecting a state that should have been turned off or cleaned up.

default.q.15day_n3-t85-q37.why.1: ✓ (b) The structure 「V-ます + っぱなし」means leaving a state unchanged when it should have been ended or dealt with, such as leaving the TV on without turning it off. It fits the context perfectly.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q37.why.2: ✗ (c) The ending 「～たて」 indicates that something has just been completed and is still fresh, as in freshly cooked rice or a newly baked cake; it does not express maintaining a state.

The pattern 「Aな + ことに」 is placed at the beginning of a clause to express the speaker’s feelings or attitude toward the situation that follows.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q38.explanation: The pattern 「V-た / A-い / A-な + ことに(は)」is usually placed at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize the speaker's subjective emotion or evaluation—such as regret, happiness, or surprise—toward the event or information that follows. The complete sentence means: "Sadly, I hear that the restaurant I often go to is about to close." To distinguish it from choice (a), 「〜かぎり」, remember that 「〜かぎりだ」usually comes at the end of a sentence to express an extreme degree of emotion, whereas 「〜ことに」comes before the clause describing the event. default.q.15day_n3-t85-q38.why.1: ✓ (b) The structure 「Aな + ことに」is grammatically and semantically appropriate for expressing regret upon hearing that a familiar restaurant is about to close.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q38.why.2: ✗ (c) The particle 「さえ」means “even,” and 「残念でさえ」does not form the correct grammatical structure for an adverbial phrase at the beginning of the sentence.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q38.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜だけ」means “only” or “just” and does not form an exclamatory expression at the beginning of a sentence modifying the entire following clause.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q39.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 降らないうちに

In the test context, the complete sentence means: “There are so many dark clouds. Let’s hurry home before it starts raining.” Example: 「温かいスープが冷めないうちに、どうぞ召し上がってください。」(Please enjoy the soup while it is still hot, before it gets cold.) default.q.15day_n3-t85-q39.why.2: ✗ (c) The grammar pattern 「うちに」 describes taking advantage of a situation before it changes and does not combine with the past form 「V-た」.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q39.why.3: ✗ (d) The past negative form 「V-なかった」cannot be combined with 「うちに」in this N3 grammar pattern.

✅ Correct answer: (c) りっぱな
The word「立派」is correctly read as「りっぱ」because of gemination and rendaku.

default.q.15day_n3-t85-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) Incorrect because combining 「立」with「派」produces the geminate consonant 「っ」, not the long vowel 「い」.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q40.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 行くたびに
The grammar pattern 「～たびに」 describes a repeated action that occurs each time the event in the preceding clause takes place.

It indicates that whenever the event in the first clause occurs, the event in the second clause also occurs as a repeated habit or predictable rule. In the sentence, it means: "Every time my mother goes to the post office, she buys some beautiful stamps." Compare: 「父は旅行に行くたびに、家族にお土産を買ってくれる。」(Every time my father travels, he buys souvenirs for the family.) When the second clause describes a repeated action that occurs whenever the first clause does, choose 「～たびに」. default.q.15day_n3-t85-q40.why.0: ✓ (a) The pattern 「V-る + たびに」 expresses the rule that every time the mother goes to the post office, she buys beautiful stamps and brings them home.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q40.why.1: ✗ (b) 「V-た + ところ」expresses that something has just been completed or that a result occurred after trying something; it is not used to indicate a repeated habit.

default.q.15day_n3-t85-q40.why.3: ✗ (d) 「V-て + ばかり」means doing nothing but a particular activity all day, usually with a critical nuance. It is unsuitable in both meaning and the sequential structure required here.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q41.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 休みがち
The grammar pattern 「Vます＋がち」expresses a tendency to repeatedly engage in an action or experience a state, often negatively. It fits the context of frequently being absent from school and making others worry.

default.q.15day_n3-t85-q41.why.2: ✗ (c) The structure Vます＋かけ describes an action that has been started but remains unfinished; it is not used to talk about the frequency of absences or missing school.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q41.why.3: ✓ (d) The grammar pattern 「Vます＋がち」means that something negative tends to or frequently does happen, accurately expressing the tendency to miss school often.
default.q.15day_n3-t85-q42.verdict:
